speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: ONTARIO-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF NUCLEAR-ELECTRIC STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members that the premier of Ontario and the chairman of Ontario hydro are today announcing in Toronto that Ontario hydro has decided to build a one million kilowatt nuclear-electric power station. This project is the second largest nuclear power station planned anywhere in the world.
This decision is a major landmark for Canada in two respects. Ontario hydro has selected the type of nuclear power station that has been pioneered and developed by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Also, Ontario hydro will build this station as a commercial venture. The two earlier and smaller nuclear power stations in Canada near Chalk River and at Douglas point on lake Huron were, in large measure, prototypes for purposes of experiment and demonstration.
By reason of the contingent financial risk in building a very large nuclear power station at this relatively early stage in nuclear development, participation by governments was desirable. No full sized nuclear power station of this type is yet in operation, so there remains a slight measure of uncertainty today as to how well they will perform. This will change when the 200,000 kilowatt nuclear power station at Douglas point, which will soon be completed, has shown that it operates successfully.
Agreement has been reached among the federal government, the Ontario government and Ontario hydro regarding the financing of this project. The estimated cost of the nuclear power station is $266 million, and this money will be subscribed by the three parties as follows. Ontario hydro will be responsible for an amount equal to the cost of the coal burning power station of the same capacity they are building at Lambton, estimated to be $120 million. The balance will be subscribed by the two governments in the ratio of 1.2 to 1, with the federal government advancing the larger portion. In terms of the present estimates of cost the federal government will subscribe $79.5 million and the Ontario government $66.5 million. It is anticipated that the capital advanced by the parties will be fully repaid with interest at normal rates out of the net operating revenues of the station. There is a good possibility of profit in government investments and reduced costs in the production of power. If all goes as planned, base load nuclear power will be cheaper than electricity generated from coal burning stations in the Ontario hydro system.
The location of the station has not yet been decided. As hon. members will know, the atomic energy control board has to be satisfied regarding safety and other aspects of any nuclear power plant for location at a particular site before it will issue a permit for construction. The board will wish to make a careful study of the proposed plant design before approving a specific site location.
I am sure all members of the house will share my deep satisfaction that the energetic and imaginative efforts of the federal government, through Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, to bring Canada to the fore in the field of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, has led and is leading to constructive and profitable undertakings of this kind.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: ONTARIO-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF NUCLEAR-ELECTRIC STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a most interesting announcement by the Minister of Industry, and I am sure everyone in Canada will be delighted. The atomic energy program, which has been operating in Canada now for about 20 years, has proved a major success. Successive governments have shown equal interest in this type of development.
7052	HOUSE OF
Construction of Nuclear Power Stations In 1958, when we had the privilege of holding office and the problem of the development of atomic energy in Canada was under consideration, acting on the advice of the highly skilled personnel of Atomic Energy and using our own judgment we decided that we would advance the program by two years, which we did, taking a calculated risk that the development of the use of natural uranium and heavy water would really fulfil the expectations of our highly competent scientists.
That paid off, and our program was advanced. The nuclear development program has been operating the small nuclear reactor near Chalk River for almost three years now, and it is the basic plant to indicate the cost of producing power by this means. As a result of that decision which we made some years ago CANDU, the larger plant near Kincardine, has gone ahead and I think is to be in operation in 1965, working according to plan.
This new announcement is further confirmation of the successful work of our atomic energy scientists, who deserve the thanks of all Canada for what they have done over the years. Their activities have been observed by the world. Other nations working with a different type of uranium-enriched uranium -and other modifying agents, were perhaps earlier in the field, but they have come to see that natural uranium plus heavy water is likely to be the most economical method of producing electric power through the use of atomic energy.
The government of India and governments of other countries in the world are interested in Canada's satisfactory experiment, and I think we have a great future in the export of our knowledge with regard to this method of producing power. Almost every country is now power hungry. Even in our own country the supply of hydroelectric power has about reached its limit except in respect of a few major developments that may be under way. With the steady increase year after year in the demand for electric power I think this method will provide the answer, and in the long run it will relieve Canada, and certainly the province of Ontario, from dependence upon the import of United States coal for steam power stations. It has been estimated that by 1980, I believe, if we did not have this other source of power we would have to expend about $300 million a year for the import of United States coal. So the balance of payments will eventually be affected to our advantage.


I am sure everybody welcomes this announcement by the minister, and I should like to pay my tribute to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, with which I have worked for a number of years, and to the scientists who, working here in Canada, have produced something which has received world wide attention and has proved a great success.

maintopic: ONTARIO-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF NUCLEAR-ELECTRIC STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party wish to join in expressing a word of commendation to the Minister of Industry, to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and to all those responsible for concluding this agreement. We feel this is another forward step in developing the use of atomic energy for the generation of electric power.
At the present time experiments are going on in various parts of the world in the field of atomic energy plants. At the present time the cost per unit is still uneconomic compared to hydro and thermal power, where there is cheap fuel available. But undoubtedly the cost of both hydro power and thermal power plants is going up, and with additional research in the field of atomic energy the costs in this field are going down. Undoubtedly the time is coming fairly soon, and I think engineers estimate that time at between ten and 12 years, when atomic energy will be competitive. We look forward to the day when we will build a national power grid in Canada, in which we will make use of hydroelectric power, harnessed tidal power, using atomic power particularly for peaking purposes. This would round out our whole power picture in Canada.
This is certainly a field of endeavour in which government planning and public enterprise can play a very important part in industrial development. This is certainly one of the legitimate fields for public enterprise and government planning. We commend the minister for this forward step and wish him every success in this undertaking.

maintopic: ONTARIO-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF NUCLEAR-ELECTRIC STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we too share in the approval that has been expressed of such an agreement as has been announced today, as it relates to the production of power. It is to be noted that this project indicates the tremendous advance that Canadian scientists have made toward the economic development of nuclear power. Not only does it relate to our ability to produce reactors, but also to our scientists who have improved methods that make economical and practical the function of such reactors.

I note that this new project is going to mean a tremendous increase in the demands for uranium and heavy water. Certainly it will have widespread effects throughout our economy. I note too that the power to be produced by this project will feed into the area around the city of Toronto. I would refer to the need we have in this country for a national power grid, and I trust that the government is taking steps to bring about discussions with the provinces on such a project, because we will not have economic use of the electricity produced unless we do have a national grid.
I am somewhat concerned about the cost involved in this project. I note that it is going to cost the federal government some $80 million in addition to what will be raised by the other two contracting parties. This brings up the point again that money used in this way for public purposes falls into the category of social capital, and that there really is no need for the cost of such projects to be doubled as far as the taxpayers are concerned before they are paid off if we would make a few adjustments in our financial setup.
Again, Mr. Speaker, we would commend the minister for concluding this agreement. We trust that further developments to meet the need for electricity in the rest of the country as well will go forward on an even more satisfactory basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives us pleasure to join with the spokesmen for the other parties in saying how glad we are to have heard the announcement just made by the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury). We are happy to find that the government has decided to provide funds for the construction of atomic power plants.
We wish to support the government's efforts in the development of such power plants for peaceful purposes. We hope Canada will play a leading role in the use of the atom for works of peace and that people will finally stop thinking of this famous atomic power only in terms of destruction, so that the human race may some day benefit from this marvellous gift God has given to man.

The house resumed, from Wednesday, August 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.

Mr. Speaker, it was just one week ago today that the hon. member for Regina City moved his subamendment listing four possible alternatives that might appear on a plebiscite if one were held on the flag. In the first six days
Canadian Flag
after the debate started there was one speaker from the Liberals for every Conservative speaker, and each of the other parties put forward three speakers. However, in the last five days the type of debate has changed somewhat, in that the Conservatives have been putting up most of the speakers while the Liberal party has contented itself with two and the other parties with one each.
I suggest that one of the big changes that has come about because of the subamendment is a recognition by those on the government side of the house, in the press gallery and across the country that the debate on the flag has been dignified by very powerful speeches. One reason these speeches have had quite an impact is that people are now beginning to recognize that they are sincere expressions springing from the minds and hearts of the people who are speaking. These are not delaying speeches. Those members who have spoken are not only speaking for their constituencies but are speaking from the depths of their beings. This is why an impact is beginning to be felt not only in this house and in the press gallery but all across the country, and the realization is spreading that we are debating a most important subject in the history of Canada.
On June 30 I took part in the debate on the original amendment and at that time, thinking ahead to what future amendments might be moved, I used these words as found on page 4887 of Hansard:
I am not going to delve into the intricate problems of the wording of the plebiscite.
I used those words because, as hon. members who may wish to read my speech at that time will see, I was aware that one of the great arguments for a plebiscite was to give the people of the country the feeling that regardless of the variety of their opinions, they would be able to indicate their feelings to the government through a plebiscite. The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City lists four choices on which the people of the country can focus their minds so the government of the day may have a realistic indication of where the weight of public opinion lies with regard to each of these choices.
When discussing the subamendment yesterday the hon. member for Oxford made a suggestion that aroused considerable interest among those of us who were listening. After

Canadian Flag
listing the four alternatives in the subamendment he suggested that once the government had an idea of how the people felt about these alternatives, the government would then be able to see more clearly what they should do. He suggested a small committee of all parties in the house, and this suggestion immediately attracted interest and questions from every party in the house.
I should like to take the suggestion of the hon. member for Oxford and say to the government that rightly or wrongly they have got themselves into a mess on the subject of the flag. If hon. members will read the speech from the throne they will see there is not a single word in it about the intention of the government to bring forward a resolution on the flag, let alone three. It is obvious that some time after the writing of the speech from the throne somebody came up with a brilliant public relations idea. They said to themselves, we are in trouble on several matters before the house, we cannot get agreement with the provinces on several of our proposals, so let us create a great smokescreen by bringing up the issue of the flag and having a long debate on it which will give us time to resolve our differences with the provinces and get our material ready for the house, and maybe make the people forget the difficulties we were in during the first few weeks of this session.
Whoever proposed that idea must accept the responsibility for having led the party he supports into probably one of the most desperate traps into which this country has ever seen a government fall. They are in a desperate situation because of the trap into which they have fallen, in that at a time in Canada's history when everybody should be working toward unity the government unwittingly has introduced a subject that is divisive.
It is the responsibility not only of the government but of all responsible members of the opposition to try to suggest some way for the government to get out of the mess and the trap in which they now find themselves. We on our part have tried to suggest that one way out is by some form of plebiscite. We have been explicit to the degree that we have outlined four potential choices that should be included in the plebiscite. There may be others.
The hon. member for Oxford has gone one step further, and I think his suggestion should be considered by the government. Whether they like it or not, whether the country likes it or not, we in Canada are in

a situation today that has explosive potentialities and no one wants to exploit that situation. The government are faced with three or four major decisions. A plebiscite is one way in which they can turn over the decision to the people. Ordinarily members of parliament do not favour the idea of a plebiscite as a good way to decide issues, but sometimes an exception has to be made in the case of moral or emotional issues.
When I spoke on June 30 I gave the precedent of the conscription debate. If I had been a member of the house in 1942 when that debate took place I think on the basis of the material before me and my knowledge of the facts I would probably have spoken against the idea of holding a plebiscite. But looking back with a historical perspective we realize now that, regardless of the logic of holding or not holding a plebiscite in that explosive situation, the plebiscite did serve to lessen the cleavage in our country.
When the time came for conscription to be enforced in Canada, the Canadians of English speaking background and of French speaking background who had been opposed to conscription accepted the will of the majority and served their country with distinction. They could do that because in spite of their opposition to conscription, the majority had spoken and they themselves had been given an opportunity to express their will.
We have put forward to the government, therefore, one way out of the difficulty, and that is the plebiscite. We have been explicit in connection with the plebiscite by outlining four choices that could be made. Now the hon. member for Oxford has outlined one more way out of the difficulty. I should like to expand that idea and add one major new ingredient. We know the government have to lose face in this situation, but that is their responsibility for getting into the mess. We have some responsibility on this side for helping them to lose as little face as possible, because this is a subject that concerns the very deep emotions of the people of this country.
I am suggesting to the government that they should consider the idea of a committee of all parties of this house. It need not be a large one. It should be small enough to do the job in several months yet big enough to encompass the opinions of all parties. In a democracy you can come to virtually unanimous agreement. I am positive, knowing the members of the house on all sides, that we can come up with something on which we can all agree. I know there has to be a

willingness to see the other person's point of view. I know there can be no compromise on principles, but within those principles you can make adjustments. Nothing has been said during this whole debate across Canada which means we have to throw up our hands and say this is a complete impasse. If we allow people to talk together long enough, to meet with each other, then with reasonable good will we will be able, as we have in the past, to arrive at a solution to the impasse. We have no less belief and we have no less good faith toward our country today than we have had in the past.
I suggest that the idea put forward by the hon. member for Oxford might be a course the government could consider even before a plebiscite. I think I can speak for many members in this house when I say that we would be willing to accept this. However, the minimum demand for accepting this idea and closing up this house while the committee went to work would be that the government thoroughly understand four simple principles. The first principle is that, regardless of the pride of anybody, this flag must be something upon which the majority of Canadian people could unite. It must not be any sort of party symbol, because that will divide us for generations. It must be something on which we in this house and the people of this country can find virtual unanimity.
Furthermore, as part of this suggestion that the government join with us in setting up an all-party committee, there should be agreement by the parties going into this committee that they would support the conclusions of the committee if those conclusions are virtually unanimous. We cannot expect complete unanimity in a committee. If there is that willingness to agree beforehand, if there is that acceptance of the fact that the political realities of Canada demand we recognize these four principles which I am listing, then I think we can get out of this situation. Yes, there will be some loss of face here and there. If we do succeed in getting an almost unanimous opinion from this committee I am positive the majority of people will follow along. We do not want to divide Canada. We want a united Canada.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

I wonder if I may conclude my four points; then at the end of my speech I will welcome any questions.
The second principle I have to emphasize has already been stated by the Leader of
Canadian Flag
the Opposition. If we are to remain true to our background and our cultures, then any flag that brings unity must afford some recognition of our past history. This country was originally a colony of France and also several colonies under the British king. We have seen a slow evolution in growth from colony to nationhood. This is the warp and woof of our history. Without conflict we were able to come to the point where the descendants of these two founding races could live together. We have come to this point where we can live together because we have always honoured a declaration which was made in the eighteenth century by Governor Carleton that the language and religion of the French speaking members of this new country would always be honoured and protected. This is the foundation upon which the country of Canada was built and has continued to build. We must always, as good Canadians, remember the pledge that was made to the French Canadians at the time of the seven years war, that we would always honour their religion and their language.
We have been able to develop economically in this country to the point where we rank with the top five or six nations of the world. With the tremendous resources that we have, with the business and scientific know-how we are developing, our future is unlimited in a material sense. This material future must not be impeded by getting into the type of struggle or confrontation that nobody wants. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, this is the second principle; that any flag that is going to create unity in Canada must contain symbols of the past. To me it is not a concession to those of English speaking background that their symbols be on the flag; to me it is not a concession that the symbols of our French speaking fellow Canadians be on the flag. So far as I am concerned this committee would have my blessing and full support if it gave equal rights to both founding races on that flag.
No superior race or cultural group; no inferior cultural group; is that too much to ask? Is it too much to ask that the flag of our country should tell the story of how people from two different language groups came, for various reasons, to this continent, have learned to live together and intend to live together?
And we intend to live together by making certain that nothing of the culture of one group shall be destroyed. We are proud, and we should be proud, of the cultural inheritance we have received. So the second principle is that there shall be recognition of the

Canadian Flag
cultural beginnings of our country. It can be done and these, I think, are reasons why it should be done.
When I was speaking on June 30 and thinking along these lines I used these words:
I think if the people looked at this situation with all the political realities as they are-and the whole country both east and west wants this country more united-here is one way that I suggest would help. Whether there is going to be, if this plebiscite idea is accepted, a committee of intellectuals, a committee of this house, or even a committee representing the provincial governments, regardless of what type of group you get together to plan the bare terms of this plebiscite I think a plebiscite could be worked out whereby the great majority of these people who now feel they are a minority would feel they had a chance to express themselves.
I felt then, and I feel today, great faith in the democratic process. If you get people together, regardless of their political party or the colour of their skin, and they fail to find their way out of an impasse, then there is a lack of genuine democratic feeling somewhere. Now we have a history of democracy in this country which goes back a long time. We can solve the present difficulty as we have solved worse difficulties in the past. I say this to hon. members who distinguish themselves by speaking very rarely in the house. I am trying to put forward a proposal which will get the government off a hook of its own making. I suggest that if we were willing to agree to set up a committee, and if we could agree to accept the decision of that committee, then providing these principles were honoured-

Is there any great difficulty about honouring the principle that there should be recognition of the traditions of both the founding races?
The third principle which I think I should put forward has received relatively little attention during the course of this debate. I say that if we are to use a committee in place of the suggested plebiscite, such a committee would have to accept as a term of reference the proposition that there must be something of religious significance on the flag. We have nothing against a maple leaf as a Canadian symbol. What shocked many of us about this proposal of a flag with three maple leaves or a single maple leaf was the loss of a symbol which we have held most dear in western civilization for 800 or 900 years. When our ancestors gathered on the deserts of the eastern Mediterranean, trying to secure control for the Christian world over the home of Christianity, they had to find symbols around which

to rally, so they picked different crosses. I am not ashamed of that, Mr. Speaker. Apart from the pennants of the knights and the nobles, this was the first use of flags on a major scale. These symbols, whether chosen by men from Britain or France or Germany, were the first in western Europe, and ever since our flags have borne something of a religious character to remind us of the history of western civilization.
I think this principle has to be followed by the Canadian people. When this matter comes to be considered in every home and in every church in Canada I do not think the people will be as happy with a flag which lacks any religious significance as they would be with one containing something to remind them that we are a part, if a small part, of western civilization with its Christian heritage.
I say this without any sense of pride or superiority for any religion. I say it simply because a nation without some realization that there is a power greater than material power lacks a necessary ingredient of greatness, both in this world today and in the future. Unless we submit to the realization that mankind is not perfect; unless we submit ourselves in all humility to the truth that there is only one power which is perfect, namely Godhead itself, a vital element is missing from our civilization. If we were ever to think that we in our mortal lives are capable of solving every problem, we would be running into grave danger. Unless we have sufficient humility of spirit to accept that on our symbols there should be a sign of superior power we are likewise sacrificing an important part of ourselves. These symbols may have weakened over the centuries, but there is still recognition in them of a power greater than we possess on this earth. So the third proposal is that any flag which would meet the terms of reference must be a flag of religious significance to some degree.
The fourth principle will be hard to explain, but I must try. Previous speakers have mentioned that ours is an evolutionary flag; it is not a revolutionary flag. I wish to draw attention to the significance of that suggestion before proceeding to consider another principle which I think we must accept. If we are to achieve the unity which we desire and which is necessary-this 80 per cent or 90 per cent unity in Canada-we must recognize that whether we like it or not this is a country of minorities. One minority, the French speaking Canadians, have always felt compelled to fight for their culture whenever

they felt it was under attack. They have developed such a consciousness of this culture that they sometimes overlook the fact that the English-or les anglais, as they call us-* are also a minority. French speaking Canadians, to use round figures, represent roughly one third of the population of this country. Canadians with English speaking backgrounds also represent roughly one third of the population. Now there are some six million new Canadians, or descendants of new Canadians, in this country, and they come from countries where other languages are spoken.
So we are all minorities. The political reality, therefore, is that we must always be careful when dealing with things which affect the spirit and the culture of our people. This means that we have to move slowly. We have got along so far because we have always protected the rights of French speaking Canadians as to their religion and language. We can get on in future if each minority group respects the basic needs of the others. One of the things which the Anglo-Saxon minority holds dear is the presence of its national symbol on the flag. This is simply a political reality.
The hon. member for Ontario spoke in this debate the other day in answer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He used an expression then which I hope will not pass unnoticed. He said he felt sorry as he saw his French speaking fellow Canadians in a confrontation with his English speaking fellow Canadians. As I read that statement, to his mind there is a confrontation between English speaking and French speaking Canadians, but that is not the way the French Canadian sees this question, Mr. Speaker, if I read the French newspapers correctly. The elite of the French Canadian editorial writers are pointing out-
Why don't you let your French members speak on this question?
Why don't you?

-the fight that is going on among English speaking Canadians. They see the English speaking people of Canada divided. They say that this matter of a flag is not one of life and death to the French Canadian; he has many more serious problems to worry about. To realize this, one has only to consider the economic living standards of the people of rural Quebec and those of the workmen in the cities and towns of Quebec.

And the unemployment in Quebec.

These are the French Canadian's worries. Certainly he would like a flag, if he is asked, I suppose, along the line that has been proposed by the government; but it is not a serious matter to him, according to the writers in the French Canadian newspapers. But read the English newspapers, Mr. Speaker. I refer, for example, to the newspapers of Alberta which supported the Liberal party in the last election. They say this proposed new flag is a massive concession to Quebec; that Quebec people insist on this new flag. But they do not insist on it, if you can believe the French Canadian newspaper writers; and the French Canadian today is wondering what all this fuss is about. It is said that the Quebec people feel the government should get out of this mess and go on to other things. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest in the face of the political realities that exist today in Canada we have an opportunity to lay down a pattern for future behaviour in matters of this sort that will stand us in good stead for many years to come.
I have mentioned this fourth principle, for example. Anything we do in Canada affecting the culture of our minorities must be of an evolutionary nature. One of the great dangers that I see in the present technique of this government is that they have put before this house a simple resolution designed to change the flag of Canada. They have decided something that affects the deep moral and emotional feeling of a great segment of our nation, one of our great cultural groups; and by way of a simple resolution they have decided this flag is going to be our national flag, regardless of the fact that probably 35 per cent of the people of Canada very sincerely want something else that is part of their whole culture and tradition.
Perhaps we have a precedent in this regard. Let us go back to the words of a former prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. If my memory serves me correctly he said that by a simple resolution we could change the constitution of this country with regard to language.
That was in 1950.

My colleague says that was in 1950. If we are going down this slippery slope of letting simple resolutions decide matters which so deeply affect minorities, we will always be in a state of alert in this country. I sometimes wonder, when we know that discussions are to be held among the federal and provincial governments on the constitution,

Canadian Flag
whether one of these evolutionary steps could not be taken with regard to something that is missing from the British North America Act. I wonder whether the discussion should not only concern changing our constitution but should not also deal with a matter such as the flag, which is now so deeply a part of most of us. Should not the question of the flag be included in any change in our constitution and incorporated therein? It could be changed, but slowly and in an evolutionary way, without forcing a minority to its knees.
I have spoken at some length on these four principles, Mr. Speaker. I am going to repeat them. I would like to say to my hon. friends opposite that I put these principles forward with the realization that they commit me, and I think many of my colleagues here, to the acceptance in advance of a decision by a committee. If we are willing to accept this, the only limitations are the four principles I have mentioned; and surely we are all good enough Canadians that we can accept those four principles. Here they are. The first is unity, in order to get a virtually unanimous opinion on this question. In spite of all the cynicism I know this is possible. These four principles are broad enough for anybody who loves his country to accept. Unity means that you get virtually unanimous support in this committee. As I have said, I think it can be done, not in 60 years but in four or five months.
The second principle is that the symbols of our past should be on that flag, and that the symbols of the two founding races should be given equal place. There is no question of one group appeasing another and people saying that one group represents one third of our people and the other two thirds. This matter concerns our history, and you do not measure quantitatively how many there are in each group. It can be done, Mr. Speaker, if we accept equal recognition, with no superior group and no inferior group. If this is done I believe we can achieve virtual unanimity all across the country as well as in a committee.
The third principle, which I trust every member of this house supports, is that on the flag there has to be something of religious significance of this nation, because without that there is nothing ahead of us; we are just-without mentioning any names-in the position in which many of the new nations of the world find themselves, with no background, no common series of principles on which they can unite. As a result they have great difficulty building a nation.

The fourth principle is very important for the future. We must accept the fact that with regard to matters on which minorities feel very deeply there must be evolutionary change, as opposed to revolutionary change. If you bring in a simple resolution such as we have before us to change a symbol that is so dear to the hearts of many of us-a flag- and force this down our throats, you will leave in Canada a near irreconcilable minority for at least a generation; and I know whereof I speak. The period of irreconcilability may be much longer.
We are suggesting that these four principles be used as terms of reference, to give the government a chance to close off this debate, to get something moving forward so that we may have a distinctive national flag, to get back to those matters that were contained in the speech from the throne, and bring unity to this country. I think these principles deserve consideration, Mr. Speaker.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, who will be dissatisfied with this type of proposal? Who will suffer from these four principles? First of all, I know the extremists will, and there are extremists on all sides. Second, those who want separation between the two founding races will be disgruntled. Third, those who believe in a republic will be dissatisfied; but there are not many republicans in Canada. Fourth, the communist party will feel dissatisfied because they want a flag which has no religious significance, and they do not want anything at all on the flag which refers to the fact that the French and English had a colonial background. We are proud of the fact that we have grown from a colony to full nationhood so peacefully and under evolutionary techniques.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that very few would feel disgruntled at this type of situation. And if I might just descend to the depths for a moment, there is another little group that will be dissatified; that is all these private enterprise friends of one or two members who are producing these new flags. They will have to call them all back in and lose a little money. However, I do not worry about them.
I suggest that if we keep these principles alive in our minds and accept the fact that the political reality today is that we are all minority groups; if we want to set an example of living together here, not only for our own satisfaction but for the whole world- we have done this in the past and we think we can do it in the future-then one of the courses open to the government is to hold a

plebiscite. But if that is unpalatable to the government, then here is another suggestion which we have made, namely that this question be referred to a committee.
I should like to thank the members of the press gallery who in the last few days have been indicating to the people of the country that those of us who are speaking in this debate believe in what we are saying. I think this is right. We know now that we are speaking for our history and our principles, and we shall continue to do so regardless of the personal cost to each one of us. We cannot and we will not retreat beyond the principles I have just enunciated. Just as our fellow French Canadians cannot and will not retreat when their culture is attacked, so do some of us who are another minority refuse to change our minds on this essentially fundamental matter. I feel that if all good Canadians fight for the rights of those who have these feelings about their culture, to protect that culture, then this country can go forward.
I hope this suggestion which I have made, one week after the hon. member for Regina City moved his subamendment listing the four choices, will be accepted. This suggestion was originally proposed by the hon. member for Oxford as a follow-up to a plebiscite. I have now proposed that this step should be considered even ahead of a plebiscite, and I put it forward as a second alternative to enable the government to get out of the mess they are in. Because there is only one other choice, a choice that we all know no one wants, and that is that we go back to the country and fight this matter out in the wildest dogfight of Canada's history. And we will split this country as a result.
The country demands of us all-not only the opposition but the government as well- some effort to clear this situation away. You cannot get out of it now without losing some face. The flag was never mentioned in the speech from the throne. Hon. members opposite are in this mess through their own fault, and they will have to make some concessions to get out of it. But I am telling them now that I am not speaking in this way just because I am a Conservative; it is because I believe that my background and the background of many millions like me gives me the right as a minority to demand, and to always demand, that on the flag of this country there be something to represent the contributions we have made to this country in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I made my proposal to the government in the hope that the leader of the government, who has some responsibility as the real house leader, would come before the meeting of the leaders of all parties with some tangible suggestion. I have put forward the proposal together with the terms of reference, but I think it is up to the Prime Minister to take some type of leadership. I have been putting forward an idea which I took from the hon. member for Oxford in the hope that it would receive serious consideration.

Mr. Speaker, for the past three weeks we have been having a single debate, that on the resolution to give Canada a distinctive national flag. During those three weeks, we have heard very few members from the province of Quebec, and I think that many factors may be instrumental in the lack of participation of the Quebec members in the said debate, up to now.
We were quite aware, we from Quebec in particular, of the scope of the problem and of the discussions which the government proposal would stir up, and we did not want to add in any way to the discussion.
But I believe, following everything which was said since the beginning of the debate, that the time has come for us to break the silence we have kept so far, in this corner of the house in particular, in order to express another point of view and to bring, if possible, a little relaxation in this august assembly.
I must admit, although I recognize that all hon. members have the right to speak freely in the house, that one must be really thickskinned not to jump out of one's seat upon hearing some of the arguments put forward since this debate started.
If I were sarcastic and mean, I could rejoice because we have witnessed since the beginning of this debate what looks like a fight to the finish between some English speaking elements. We have been used in the past to seeing French Canadians fight among themselves, discuss things fiercely, sometimes disagree deeply, but this time we are witnessing this disagreement within the country's English element.

But, Mr. Speaker, this does not make me happy, any more than I rejoice or will ever rejoice to see disunity among people of the same ethnic group.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think we could be happy with such a situation.
I will surely not try to refute all that has been said but there is one particular point on which I should like to set the record straight. On several occasions and no later than last night, some hon. members stated that the flag resolution is a surrender to the province of Quebec and that the Liberal party is selling the red ensign for the 75 Quebec votes.
Nothing could be farther from the truth, Mr. Speaker. Like their fellow Canadians, the people of Quebec have long been waiting for a distinctive flag; consequently, they are not the only ones who wish to have such a flag. Indeed, if the new distinctive flag is not accepted throughout Canada by the majority of the people, Quebec will not know what to do with it. It will just become another half kept promise probably carried out to get more votes.
Mr. Speaker, we would not know what to do with a flag which would not meet with the approval of the majority of Canadians, and if it is to be flown only in the province of Quebec, we do not want it. Our province already has its own flag and if we advocate the adoption of a distinctive flag for Canada, it is because we are convinced that the time has come to show some national pride and maturity.
If there is any one here who thinks that the Liberal members from Quebec were elected because of such a vague promise, let me tell him that he is sorely mistaken.
On the other hand, if some Liberal members from Quebec think they will be reelected just because a new flag has been adopted, let me tell them that the people of our province have a most disagreeable surprise in store for them.
The Liberals are not entitled to any gratitude on the part of the Quebec people if they give them that so-called flag. That gratitude has already been expressed through the heavy vote Quebec has given the Liberals in the past following the many promises made on each occasion.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, if the Liberals think the problems of Quebec, as well as those of Canada as a whole, are going to be solved simply by means of the flag issue, they are bound to find out that those problems are much too complex to be settled merely by adopting the flag.

It was claimed for a long time that this matter of a flag was of the utmost importance to the Quebec people. But, to back the point I am making, let me refer to certain achievements of the Conservatives, when they were in office. The Conservatives have indeed given simultaneous translation to the House of Commons, requested so many times and even promised in the past. Has it helped the election of Conservatives in Quebec? No, Mr. Speaker, because today Quebec is aware that its problems will not be settled by symbols only. Its problems, like those of the whole country, go much deeper than that.
Mr. Speaker, should Quebec favour Liberal candidates at the next general election, it will surely not be because of the popularity of the Liberal party, but because the opposition parties will have failed to express their views and offer a much better solution to our present problems. If the Liberals win the next election, I think that it will be due to the weakness of the opposition.
Mr. Speaker, I have always been a strong supporter of any proposal to give national symbols to our country.
Today, the circumstances are such that I am one of those who are entrusted in this house with the extremely difficult task of voting on those symbols, at a time in our history when tensions between the various ethnic groups which constitute the Canadian people are such as to jeopardize the very basis of our institutions.
It is generally admitted that confederation survived thanks to compromises accepted by Quebec and for which we, the people of Quebec, unfortunately had to pay day in and day out.
Judging from the various viewpoints expressed throughout Canada as well as in this house, one would tend to wonder if the time was well chosen to start the discussion on this legislation which more than any other one is likely to bring a discussion based only on emotions and unfortunately to give some demagogues free rein to show their true colours, if not their skill.
Personally, I feel that there is nothing to be gained by further delaying the choice of a flag and that, on the contrary, this shock treatment-since it is certainly a shock treatment-will perhaps compel all Canadians to pull themselves together and put more emphasis on the many reasons to look for a better understanding on all those matters that divide us.
Certainly I would have preferred that the resolutions which have been introduced would not mention any colonial symbols. But as I
