said, I feel that we will have to be patient and probably accept a compromise in the hope that within a few years from now the percentage of Canadians by birth will increase and that those relics will disappear by the will of the majority of the Canadian people themselves.
As for us, Canadians of French origin, who settled here more than 350 years ago, we have been 100 per cent Canadians for a long time. But we still feel interested and touched by everything concerning France. That is why, even if it may seem difficult, we must try to understand the present emotions of the seven million Canadians of British origin who are being asked today to discard another symbol of our past as a British colony, to take one more step forward on the road towards complete independence in fact and in right. I recognize that such progress is proceeding at a snail's pace, Mr. Speaker, but I would rather have it slow and well ordered than quick and the cause of chaos such as that experienced by the majority of former colonies, whether French, British or others, which, in recent years, gained their independence at the cost of bloodshed and great economic and social. upheaval.
The evolution of Canada is the result of long years of struggle which must be continued. To a certain degree, the French Canadians have been the catalyst in that progress towards complete emancipation of our country. We are being accused today, as we were in the past and as, unfortunately, we will still be for a certain time to come, of trying to divide the country, although it is completely the opposite.
We want a strong Canada, strong with the strength of all its parts, Quebec being one of them.
We are crying out against foreign control of our economy, not only in Quebec, but throughout Canada.
As our ethnic group had to fight for the last 200 years for its survival as a nation with a French culture on this American continent, we realize more than any other group, more than our Anglo-Canadian fellow citizens, the danger which the ever-growing influence of the American way of life represents, and how much it may jeopardize the future life of Canada as a separate entity. That is why, Mr. Speaker, Canada needs distinctive symbols.
I would, at this point, if I may, quote from an article written some time ago in the

Canadian Flag
Montreal Gazette. I apologize to hon. members for my English pronunciation, which is unfortunately far from perfect though I wish it were. I quote:

I am a "landed immigrant" from Britain who has lived in Canada for 12 years without bothering to take out Canadian citizenship (after all, I thought, this country flies a variation of the British emblem so obviously its citizenship must be merely a variation of British citizenship which I already had in full measure).
The day the new and distinctively Canadian flag is unfurled for the first time will be the same day I file my application papers. When I next visit England, it will be a proud moment when I can pass Canada house in London, see the Canadian flag rippling in the breeze and think: That's my flag.
I have waited 12 long years to become a Canadian with a flag, a national anthem and at least a modicum of national pride to call my own. Thanks Mr. Pearson, it looks as if I will shortly have my chance. The back of my (former English) hand to those who would deny me this chance.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the expression of view of a man who was born in England, and I feel he is not the only one to express this opinion. I hope that those who were born in Canada of English culture will be as much Canadian as this man intends to be, and support for Canada as much as possible the symbols we need so that we can be recognized as a really independent country.

Mr. Speaker, when reviewing the reasons which the Fathers of Confederation put forward to unite the various British colonies in America at the time, it is interesting to note that the first and foremost aim was to set up Canada as a distinctive country, which would be sufficiently strong to resist American assimilation. It is too bad that the matter of a truly Canadian flag was not settled then, as all those dissensions and discussions, and all those problems which we have to face today would not have come up at all. They probably expected that their successors would not delay in filling this gap, but they had not taken partisan politics into account, i.e. a state of mind which having been maintained and further developed, is now obstructing any decision on the flag.
Today, we are in a dilemma. The country seems to be hopelessly divided. But is this split really hopeless? Personally, I do not think so; I would hate to think so. No problem is hopeless when men of good will objectively decide to find a solution.

Mr. Speaker and hon. members, if ever a matter, or circumstances called for a compromise, it is those which are now under consideration. Quebec is in no way committed to the design suggested by the Prime Minister. I am certain that the French Canadian people who are conscious of their responsibilities with regard to the preservation of harmony in this country, will, once again, as they did in the past, show sound common sense in this matter.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker-and I do not intend to take more than the necessary time- I would like to appeal to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to his colleagues who support him in the house, to agree to reconsider their position, because, otherwise, they will plunge the country into a state of chaos as we have never seen before, and the result of this action could have unconceivable repercussions on the future.
Suggestions were made-one needs only to read in the Montreal Gazette the question "Do we want our flag?". And you have the former Ontario premier, Mr. Leslie Frost, who, I believe, is a good Conservative and wants to keep this unity we all want in this country. This man who is now well on in years and quite experienced in public administration, thinks that it is time for him to take a stand. He urges those who were and are still his supporters to reconsider their position and to accept a compromise.
I can appreciate the situation in which the Conservatives find themselves. They say: "This is the Liberal flag, the Pearson flag, and the rest of Canada will support him for 50 years". The Liberals, of course, have been paving the way by reminding people that conscription was passed by the Conservatives. One may expect the flag to be the cornerstone of the next election campaign, and that is why the Conservatives object to it as practical politics. On the other hand, if the Liberals expect to win the support of the province of Quebec with this flag, and if it is their only achievement, they have a very poor opinion of the Quebeckers and of their judgment, and it is high time they reconsider their position.
As far as I am concerned, I put my trust in the Quebec people, and in their judgment, and if the Liberal party comes to Quebec at the next federal election with only a Canadian flag as its achievement, let me tell you again, my dear friends, that it will be very much surprised because the Quebec people

are much more realistic and practical than they were in the past. Simultaneous translation, set up by the Leader of the Opposition, did not bring him the deep gratitude of the province of Quebec. And it is not by granting to Quebec unimportant things, which they wanted and were entitled to, that he received the support of that province. The real problem is far more complex than that.
We shall have this distinctive national flag, for the great majority of Canadian people want it. Considering that this flag may be the fruit of the longest period of gestation ever, and that, for many, great moral suffering might have accompanied its birth, I am convinced that, afterwards, all Canadians, whoever they be, will respect and cherish it. Besides, it will have been the result of many struggles and probably many concessions, valuable concessions indeed, no doubt important ones. Even if, for the good of the country, whatever party we may belong to, we have to make concessions-I am sure there will be several in the province of Quebec, and I hope as many in the other parts of Canada-I believe we shall have to make such concessions and that we should, especially we, Canadians, come to an understanding and vote unanimously in favour of what will be not the Liberal flag or the Pearson flag, but the flag of Canada.

Would the hon. member allow me a question?
Does the hon. member want to imply that due to the fact that he has decided to accept the three maple leaf flag, this flag should be accepted without allowing us to suggest other designs to the government?

Certainly not, since I spoke of compromise. This flag design is far from meeting my personal taste, which by the way is not the taste of the majority of the Quebec people. And this is quite normal. To say that this design is beautiful, far from it. But, if I were to let my personal taste prevent possibly the adoption of the flag, I think that it would be a great disservice to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting for many days for the chance to exercise my right and carry out my duty by speaking on this flag question, one of the most important issues, I believe, that has ever arisen in this country. Although I have very strong, personal feelings toward the Canadian red ensign, and probably there is no riding in Canada that feels more
Canadian Flag
strongly toward the red ensign than mine, my position is not very popular. The stand I have taken has been one of moderation, and I shall try to make my remarks here today in the same key.
I was very disappointed yesterday to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) call this debate a filibuster, particularly when the Prime Minister himself invited all members to express their opinions on this question. Many of our members have not yet had this chance. As I have said, I have been waiting for many days for my turn to speak on this question.
I am speaking specifically to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More). I shall not read the subamendment, but the gist of it is that amongst the questions to be placed on the plebiscite are the following: Would you prefer the Canadian red ensign, or the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritage of both founding races? Do you like the three maple leaf flag or the one maple leaf flag? I have five arguments I will put forward in support of this subamendment or rather in consideration of the subamendment.
My first argument, Mr. Speaker, is that this government has no mandate from the people of Canada to introduce the maple leaf flag or any such flag that they may have in mind. I have with me a full page advertisement which appeared in the Victoria Colonist dated March 31, 1963. It is headed, "Policies of the Liberal Party, General Election, 1963." In looking over this full page advertisement I see many things that the Liberals promised. Glancing through it, I see that they are going to reform taxes, which they have done by increasing them; municipal loans for schools and parks are to be provided; provide mortgages for existing homes-I will bet that got them many thousands of votes-improve rural housing; set up an economic council; assist in retraining courses for industry; provide ten thousand $1,000 scholarships; improve public financing for universities; pensions to make possible retirement on half pay at age 65 with a maximum pension of $296 per couple; $75 old age assistance for single women and widows; collective bargaining for civil servants; restore unemployment insurance fund; create a fisheries credit agency, and so on. I could take another half hour listing the things that they have promised which they have not yet done, many of which they have already decided to abandon. No matter how carefully you examine this full page advertisement which was used in many

Canadian Flag
newspapers across British Columbia, there is no reference whatever to a flag. How can the government, particularly when they were elected as a minority, presume that they have a mandate from the people to present this three maple leaf flag?
During the last election campaign I recall that the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) (Mr. Groos), now sitting in support of the government, who opposed me in 1961 and
1962,	was on the same platform with me in
1963.	I think he will confirm that in our area this flag question was not raised at all. If it had been, I am quite sure the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) would have said he was for the red ensign. This is my first reason for supporting the subamendment, that this government has no mandate from the people of Canada.
My next argument in favour of this subamendment is that if there is to be a vote on any portion of the flag question it will not be a free vote of the members of this house. At one time the Prime Minister promised a free vote. On May 12, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates), he said, as reported at page 3164 of Hansard:
When the time comes to submit the decision of the government in this matter to the House of Commons I would hope every member of the house would vote as his conscience dictates, and that there would be no question of confidence or nonconfidence in a party sense.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, somebody prevailed upon the Prime Minister to change his position. I think by then he started to hear from the people across Canada. He has stated that this is a question of confidence in the government. I maintain therefore that any vote that may be taken here will not be a free vote in which every member on that side will vote according to his conscience or in accordance with the way the people of his riding feel. To prove this contention I will cite an individual case. Unfortunately, it happens to concern a very good friend of mine, the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) (Mr. Groos). I will submit evidence to show how members on the Liberal side have changed their views, or rather how they have been brought into line-I do not say they have changed their views. I will first of all read a letter which a constituent wrote to the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.). It is a letter from a Mrs. E. E. Fox, and this is the relevant part of it:
Regarding that there are many different and decided opinions regarding this matter which is of such vital interest to all Canadians, I would urge that the red ensign be adopted as Canada's national flag; and, furthermore, that a proclamation of that flag be made without delay.

This was the letter addressed to Mr. David Groos, M.P. Now here is the reply dated February 10 from the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) to Mrs. Fox:
I thank you for your letter concerning the national flag of Canada, and for letting me know your views on this subject.
Please let me assure you that I agree absolutely with everything in your letter and I intend to do everything I possibly can to see that our present flag keeps flying.
Maybe it was in a weak moment he wrote that one. That letter was dated February 20. Eleven days later the hon. member still had not changed his mind, because he wrote another letter, the relevant part of which reads-and I will quote it:
I intend to do all within my power to retain the present Canadian flag.
Then on February 7 the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) wrote another letter to one of his constituents, as follows:
Thank you for your recent letter concerning Canada's national flag.
Just let me say I am in complete agreement with you and the many others of my constituents who have written to me in this regard, and I intend to do my utmost to see that Canada's present flag keeps flying.
Again, I apologize for having to refer to a particular hon. member but I am using this case as an example of how the whip cracks and members are brought into line on the other side. On May 21 the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) wrote a letter on the flag issue to the Victoria Daily Times and to the Victoria Colonist in which he said:
The Prime Minister will be taking action on this matter within the next few days. I am free to vote as I wish and I will, naturally, be guided by the views of the residents in my constituency.
The letter went on:
No flag will be acceptable to me unless it finds a large degree of favour right across the country-
With regard to the second part of the letter which I have read, I presume the hon. member has seen the result of the poll which shows that a majority of the people in nine out of ten of the provinces prefer the Canadian red ensign.
To revert to the first quotation I gave from the hon. member's letter, the part in which he said he would naturally be guided by the views of the residents of his constituency, 1 should like to ask: What are the feelings on this flag question of the constituents in the Victoria (B.C.) riding?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I should perhaps bring it to the attention of the hon. member that the Chair has some doubt about

the propriety of quoting letters exchanged between another member and a third person. This appears to be contrary to the spirit of debate, where an hon. member has to express his own opinions rather than the opinions of someone else, or of other members. I must say I have no authority before me on the point, but this is a matter which the hon. member might keep in mind in case he is considering reading other letters of the same type.

On the point of order, I do not think there is any authority for the proposition you have just put forward, Mr. Speaker. My understanding of the rules is the reverse and my impression at the moment is that the hon. member is perfectly within his rights in taking the attitude he has, and that he has proceeded in accordance with the rules which govern this house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid I have to reiterate I have no authority before me at the moment. I have simply expressed the understanding of the Chair of the rules which govern our debates generally-that it is not in the spirit of debate for hon. members to quote from private correspondence in which they themselves are not engaged.

I would accept your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I might just say that the person whose letter I read gave me authority to use the letter. She, of course, owns the letter once she receives it. However I have no more letters to quote. I wish to proceed with my speech. I was referring to the letter which the hon. member wrote to the Victoria Daily Times which was made public by being published in that newspaper.
What do the people of the riding of Victoria (B.C.) feel about this question. The Victoria Daily Times had a poll, and I will read from its issue of May 20, 1964, concerning this poll.
Not in recent memory has a public opinion poll conducted by the Times drawn such an intense reaction as the flag ballot.
Times readers are concerned enough it seems, that they wish to make it a sincere test ol opinion.
What was the result of this poll taken by the Victoria Daily Times? On May 29, 1964 the poll was closed. By that time 3,860 ballots had been cast. Of these, 2,847 were in favour of the red ensign and 1,013 were in favour of the maple leaf flag, that is, almost 3 to 1 in favour of the ensign.
I may say I have warned the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) that I intend to attack his position and I ask him to reply to the charges I have made. I see with satisfaction that he is making notes and I feel sure he would
Canadian Flag
like to explain to his constituents the change in his position. I am using this case just as an example to show that if there is to be a vote on any part of this flag question it will not be a free vote.
It was interesting to note that yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) said it would be a free vote. I think he was flying a balloon. But even if the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) were to tell us tomorrow that there would be a free vote it would be too late, because the whip has cracked and the members have been placed in position; they have made their stand clear and they cannot change, now. To say, now, that there will be a free vote, would be a hollow ruse.
The next argument I wish to advance in favour of the subamendment concerns the actions of this government in creating disunity and division within the country. My colleagues from Quebec know that I have always been sympathetic to their case and that I understand their problems. I myself come from a bi-racial country where my own people were in much the same position as the French speaking people consider themselves to be in Canada. I wish to make it clear that the statements I propose to read do not represent my own opinions. What I am attempting to do is to show how people in various parts of the country are reacting to the actions of this government. I am almost scared, sometimes, to see the reaction of the people to the government's proposal. I propose to quote excerpts from letters I have received, just to show how people feel, and how the government had divided the country. Here is a letter which says:
Some member of the opposition should rise to remark that Mr. Pearson is taking a course of action which will result in his place in history being that of the man who divided Canada.
Here is part of another letter:
If we are adopting this flag merely to placate a vociferous minority, we are doing a grave injustice to the rest of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I would earnestly ask the French speaking members from Quebec to listen to this to see how people in other parts of Canada feel toward them. Much of this feeling amongst these people has been created by the action of this government. I can tell the house that in 1962 I carried out a poll of my riding on this French question, and even I was surprised to learn how sympathetically the people of my riding considered the French problem. But this is not the case today.

Canadian Flag
The hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto)- who, incidentally, made a very thoughtful and thought provoking speech-said yesterday that it is only a minority of Quebeckers who are creating this trouble. He went on to say that people in the other parts of Canada do not know this. He is quite right. They read the press, and do not know this. The C.B.C. in particular is terrible in this respect. Instead of trying to place the whole question in perspective, they emphasize the actions of this extremist minority in Quebec, and the people in the rest of the country, particularly those in British Columbia, think this is the way the whole of Quebec feels. Because of the present action of this government with regard to the flag, these people are caused to say, "See, we told you so". I want to impress on my French colleagues that this is doing them harm. This letter says:
It was kind of you to show an interest in my small effort to stop the vicious plan to force on us a national flag only wanted by the lousy peasoupers.
I am very regretful, Mr. Speaker, that I have to quote this, but I am trying to convey to the government how these people feel. It is terrible that the action of this government is causing this type of bitterness. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I would hate to quote some of the letters I have received, but I have quoted these extracts in order to convince the government that their action is causing these people to feel more bitter against French Canadians. I have dozens of letters along these lines, but I think those I have quoted will suffice to make my point that the action the government has taken and the manner in which they are dealing with this question is creating disunity and division. It is causing harm to the whole country, particularly to the people of Quebec, because other people say this is done to appease Quebec.
I want to emphasize again, Mr. Speaker, that I have used these quotations to try and impress upon the government that this is how people feel. I regret it. I have a whole file of letters here from which I could quote; they are all along those lines. The fourth argument-
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
No. When I am through I will answer any questions.
You wouldn't recognize an answer if you got one.

I have a fourth argument I want to advance as to why the action of the

government and the manner in which they are dealing with this question should be abandoned in favour of the subamendment. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) has so eloquently described it, the English speaking people of British descent- most of them, at any rate-feel very, very strongly about the question of the flag. I can best demonstrate this by quoting some of the expressions used in their letters. First I should like to read an advertisement which was placed in the Victoria Daily Times of June 8. It is an advertisement for the sale of a property and it says:
Our clients along with Lord and Lady Cholmon-deley have decided that since the government of Canada has seen fit to remove the red ensign that they simply cannot live under the three maple leaves and therefore have bestowed on us the exclusive privilege of selling their lovely secluded country estate.
Oh, oh.

I will now quote from an editorial which appeared in The Province of December 16 last. It says:
But many Canadians, including thousands of veterans who fought for their country and to whom the flag has a special meaning, want to retain Canada's red ensign.
It was good enough to fight for and for some of our comrades to give their lives for, the veterans say. Leave the flag alone.
Here is another letter from one of my constituents-a former Liberal, incidentally, who has changed his political affiliations since the flag issue arose-and I quote in part:
-a desire to cater, for purely political reasons, to Quebec with its large degree of political influences.. .Does Pearson, after all the good work he has done, want to be known as the "great disrupter"?
The writer of that letter referred to Mr. Mackenzie King going down in history as the "great appeaser" and then refers to the Prime Minister being known as the "great disrupter". Here is a letter from a chap for whom I have a very high regard; he is very active in the Legion:
I enclose copy of my letter to the Prime Minister regarding the flag question, the implications of which, in my view, are far deeper and more sinister than many people realize...
I think this vicious thing should be fought against with every fibre of our being.
I have a great many other letters. Here is one from a young Canadian 16 years old:
I always felt that Canada had a flag. It is the red ensign that is recognized around the world as Canada's flag. Do we have a justifiable reason for changing this flag? There must be a reason, one might say.

And so on. The fourth argument I have used is that people feel very strongly on this question of the Canadian red ensign. I am not one of those that say it must be the Canadian red ensign or nothing. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I have been severely criticized in my riding by some of my people for not taking that stand. But this is not the attitude we on this side of the chamber take. I think the hon. member for Qu'Appelle put forward a very reasonable proposal with great sincerity when he said that we on this side are anxious somehow to arrive at a consensus on the question of a flag that will be accepted by members on all sides of the house; not just by the people of Quebec but the people from the other parts of Canada.
My last argument in support of the subamendment is that if this flag went through on the present basis, a great many Canadians would not accept it. Again, Mr. Speaker, I have many letters from individuals and groups indicating this stand. How can you introduce a flag in a manner whereby a large number of people will not accept it? Surely the government must realize this is the way people feel in some parts of Canada, and surely this must be cause for reconsideration by the government of their position. I know they are in a difficult position. In my view, this plebiscite with the four questions to be asked is an alternative. In view of the whole situation at the moment, I believe it is an alternative that might get us out of the mess in which this government has put the country. It is one alternative. I personally tend to favour the proposal made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I am not going so far as he went. He laid down four principles which could be contained in the terms of reference of the committee. I do not go so far as to say that those necessarily should be the terms of reference; I think they might be ones the committee could be asked to consider. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the flag which the committee might recommend need not necessarily conform in all respects to the four principles laid down by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. However, I think his proposal indicates that we are prepared to get together and see if we can arrive at a consensus on this question.
Two of my French colleagues on this side of the house have approached me in regard to the flag. I know they have become concerned about the position in which we find ourselves. They came to me with two flags and asked how I would react to them, knowing that I come from red ensign country. One of these flags did not have the union jack on 20220-448
Canadian Flag
it, although it bore some resemblance to it. I told both these gentlemen that if there was any kind of reasonable unanimity for such a flag in, say, an all-party committee, or for either one of those two flags, I would go for it; I would sell it in my own riding. I would do this, provided there was reasonable unanimity in the committee that considered these designs. It will be hard for me to do this, but for the sake of unity I would accept such a decision of the committee and sell it to my people, although I would be strongly criticized by a certain group. That indicates that we are prepared to find some solution. We have considered the matter, and I am sure the government must now have realized that we on this side are serious about it. Every hon. member who has spoken-and this applies to both sides-has spoken with sincerity and conviction. But this is a serious question and the government must realize that they must change their position. If they do not accept the suggestion of holding a plebiscite they should consider the idea of a committee such as that suggested by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). I am sure that even some of those on this side who have extreme feelings about the question will make an honest effort to find common ground so that this present divisive action of the government can be stopped and the people of Canada can get together and find a symbol acceptable to the majority of them. This would at least not create the strong feelings which have been aroused by the present action of this government.

Mr. Speaker, I was not unaware that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatter-ton) was going to speak on this subject. He wrote me a note yesterday and told me so. He said there was nothing personal in it but he was going to make some comments which would require some answers. I must say I am a little bit surprised at the turn his remarks took in the early part of his speech but I will answer his questions.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I am one of the less partisan politicians in this house, and I try to be so in my remarks both in this chamber and in committee. First of all, let me say that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich is quite right when he says I have been a supporter of and believer in the red ensign, and I make no apologies for that. For many years I was under the impression that this was our flag, and I have so answered when I have been queried on the subject.

Motions for Papers
As I say, I acknowledge and take full responsibility for what I said in the letters which he so helpfully produced on the floor of this house. However, I must point out that when this matter of a national flag for Canada became a great national issue I very soon became aware, as did a great many other members of this house, of the need for looking far beyond my own personal feelings, and I became aware of the need for taking a long term, detached view of this whole matter. When I did this and I had reached my own conclusion I lost no time in placing my thoughts and my views before the public in every way possible.
The people who live in Victoria are certainly in no doubt whatever as to what are my views on this point, and I have been exceedingly heartened by their reaction to my statements. I am not pretending that in Victoria public reaction is not divided on this issue, but by and large the Victorians, as I would expect, are taking a tolerant, restrained and understanding approach to this whole matter. I feel that I am competent to speak for them in this regard because I too, apart from being their member, get a fair amount of correspondence from my constituents.
I believe that many people who live in Victoria and who live across this land, now that they understand what are the proposals and have thought about the matter for a while, have changed their minds on this issue. They, like myself, have no fixed, immovable views on this matter, and certainly the volume and the content of my mail on this subject of the flag shows this to be true. In this regard I would thank the people of Victoria very much for corresponding with me on this matter and for giving me their views.
The hon. member made some reference to the fact that we are servants of the public in trying to point out what the people in our ridings are thinking. I should like to comment on that, but I notice it is now five o'clock, so may I call it five o'clock and continue with my speech at eight o'clock.

subtopic: THE GUARANTEE COMPANY OP NORTH AMERICA

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. S-37, respecting The Guarantee Company of North America-Mr. Watson (Chateauguay-Hunt-ingdon-Laprairie)-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Name in French.

subtopic: THE GUARANTEE COMPANY OP NORTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie (Mr. Watson) could give us a few explanations on this bill?

subtopic: THE GUARANTEE COMPANY OP NORTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the sole purpose of this bill is to add a French version to the

name of The Guarantee Company of North America. The French version of the name is La Garantie, Compagnie d'Assurance de l'Amerique du Nord. That is the only reason for the bill.

subtopic: THE GUARANTEE COMPANY OP NORTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in 1964, this company wants to obtain a French name. Why is that need felt today? Is it because they are aware of the awakening in Quebec since our group has been sitting in the House of Commons, as a separate group from the province of Quebec striving to have recognized the need for the French language as well as the English language? That may be one of the factors which has prompted this company to introduce this bill. That may also be the reason why this company wishes to have a French Canadian name.
There may be other factors which have some influence in that respect, namely that this North American insurance company is thinking about the possibility of developing in the province of Quebec-since they realize the existence of that nationalist trend in the province and all across Canada-in order to have rewarding operations. Maybe they think that if they print a French name on their letterhead, on statements of accounts and insurance policy forms, they will have more customers, because all that would indicate they are a Canadian company.
When there is money at stake, companies go to work. I am not against that change in name. We must even be happy to see that an English company wishes to have a French name.
We are the ones, the Creditistes, who said that we would block all bills coming from the Senate. I think we must adhere to that principle, because we say that the Senate has no right to block bills like the one concerning the bank of British Columbia, as requested by Premier Bennett, that is a bank which would enable the government of British Columbia to be master in its own house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE GUARANTEE COMPANY OP NORTH AMERICA
speechtext: Order. I must interrupt the hon. member who will admit, I am sure, that the reference he is making to another bill has absolutely no relevancy with the matter now before us.

subtopic: THE GUARANTEE COMPANY OP NORTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I was saying that only to explain our objections to Bill No. S-37 now before us.
That is the reason why we object to the third reading of this bill. We are prepared to let it pass second reading today, in the 20220-448J
Private Bills
hope that the Senate will soon decide to send us the bill we are expecting and which we want to discuss, namely the bill concerning the bank of British Columbia.
Now, if this company, established many years ago, feels that it needs a French name, we are delighted and we will permit this bill to be read a second time, but you may be sure that we shall oppose the motion for third reading. We shall oppose it, even though we are not against the bill itself, but we shall do this as a protest against the decision taken by the Senate respecting another bill.

subtopic: THE GUARANTEE COMPANY OP NORTH AMERICA
speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, as you can see from the title, the purpose of Bill No. S-38 which I have the honour to sponsor is to incorporate the Congregation of the Marist Sisters.
The congregation was founded in France on December 8, 1824. Its present field of action covers 11 countries, including Canada and more particularly the county of Madawaska in New Brunswick.
That religious congregation has always done some fine work. The Marist Sisters look after the education of the young, the ailing, the orphans and the aged and they do social and mission work. In other words, they spend their whole lives serving humanity. As outlined in section 4, the purpose of the bill is to enable the congregation to continue its work which includes the provision of educational facilities, the establishment of orphanages, convents and hospitals and to provide the congregation with the proper legal powers in that connection.
I think the hon. members will be pleased to grant its request which has already been endorsed by the miscellaneous private bills committee.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to approve the passage of this bill, namely the incorporation of the Congregation of the Marist Sisters.
As the sponsor of the bill said, that congregation was founded in France in 1824 and now it has members in 11 countries, which shows that it is in demand because of all the services it renders to society.
According to the provisions of section 4, one realizes that the community does its magnificent work at the request of various dioceses. According to the bill, it would have its headquarters in Hull. It is a central place and I think that the government will be able to give financial assistance to this community in order to establish an orphanage. There are too many youths and old people in Canada who lack the necessities of life and live in substandard housing. It would be a good thing

if a building for the aged were built on behalf of those nuns who devote all their lives to the service of others.
Under section 6, they will be authorized to purchase and own property. It is quite normal for a congregation to own the land and building where it is performing its good work. If the corporation is not authorized to own its land and its building, how can it be expected to develop.
Therefore, I congratulate that corporation for having submitted this request and we have no objection to third reading of this bill, since our group does not have five but only four members. We do not want to delay indefinitely the passing of this bill, even if it comes from the Senate, because it has priority over certain bills presented last week.

speechtext:

the second reading of Bill No. S-39, to incorporate Meota Pipe Lines Ltd.
Could we have a word of explanation?

As has been customary, a group of Canadian citizens, all residents of Edmonton, Alberta, are coming before parliament to ask for the incorporation of Meota Pipe Lines Ltd. The purpose of this company is to build a pipe line from southeastern Saskatchewan to southwestern Manitoba. Since the pipe line crosses a provincial boundary, the company must take out a federal charter. They propose to build 22 miles of pipe line, something in the neighbourhood of four inches in diameter, depending upon the size of the market available for natural gas. The pipe line is to be constructed from Gainsborough, Saskatchewan, to Melita, Manitoba.
I might add also that in asking for second reading, Mr. Speaker, it is a well established practice that bills of this nature are referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. The proposed president and general manager of the company, as well as other persons involved, are fully prepared to appear before that committee and give in greater detail the reasons for requesting this charter. If the company is fortunate enough to secure a charter, it will then have to appear before the national energy board as well as the conservation boards of the provincial governments involved. The rates to be charged, of course, are set by the provinces. The company will then have to secure a charter from Melita, Manitoba, in order to sell natural gas in that town.
The main object of this company is to transmit gas from Gainsborough to southwestern Manitoba in the hope that a market can be developed for this Canadian product. 1 might add that the people involved are all Canadian citizens and Canadian capital will be used to build the line and develop the market for this Canadian product for the greater convenience of southwestern Manitoba, which is not now served with natural gas.
If there are any further questions I shall do my best to answer them in the hope that we can proceed with this bill. I would say to those who feel they cannot pass bills of this nature in this house, that the bill will be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines and the officials

will be called to give detailed answers to any further questions hon. members might have. The bill will then come back to the house for third reading.

I just want to say on behalf of our party that we have no objection to sending this bill to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for further detailed study. It is well known that this procedure is followed. At that time the officers or petitioners, if I may call them that, for this charter will appear before the committee. Hon. members will have the opportunity of interrogating them and getting all the technical details with regard to what they propose to do with the charter.
I feel I should say one more thing. It is the practice for small oil and gas companies in western Canada to find the gas and then attempt to find markets for it. This is something that goes on all over Alberta and Saskatchewan. It would be fair to say we have dozens of pipe lines leading from the smaller gas fields to towns, villages and cities all over western Canada. This has been beneficial to the people who have developed gas wells and risked their capital to find those fields and develop them. It has always been beneficial to some of the smaller towns and villages which otherwise would never have had an opportunity to enjoy the use of natural gas. In this particular case it happens that between the gas fields and the town which will be using the gas will be a provincial boundary, and as the sponsor of the bill, or the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) speaking for him, has indicated, it is necessary therefore that the company should receive a federal charter.
There is nothing unusual about setting down a four inch pipe line for 20, 30, or 50 miles so that people farming along the way may have the benefits of natural gas in their homes or in their farms and also to provide for the needs of a small town which otherwise would not have the benefits of natural gas. It is somewhat unusual that a company must come to parliament because the line crosses a provincial border, but on behalf of this party I would recommend that the bill be sent to committee for detailed study since the arrangement underlying it is a common practice all over the western provinces.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
The house resumed from Thursday, August 6, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Konantz for the second reading of Bill No. S-6 to incorporate the Bank of Western Canada.

Before this motion is passed I should like to say a word or two. We who come from western Canada naturally have a keen interest in the establishment of a bank which might bring a great deal of benefit to us.
I may say that the world of banking has been the subject of a great deal of interest over the years on the part of western farmers generally. The banks have had a long history of opening up their vast resources to farmers, only to foreclose their loans or call for their money at the worst possible times, to the detriment of their customers. This has been the history of banking in western Canada as far as farmers generally are concerned. In recent years, it is true, many farmers have been able to take advantage of loans guaranteed by the government and in these circumstances the banks have probably been more lenient.
As I say, the people of western Canada have taken a deep interest in the banking world. It may be of passing interest to note that banking and finance have been of particular interest to the province of Alberta, from which I come, for the past 30 years. This is probably why I picked up my ears when I heard some months ago that a bank called the Bank of Western Canada was to be established. In continuation of this interest I read the reports of the committee of the Senate with regard to this bank. I must say I was somewhat shocked to find that the only thing which was western about this bank was the name. Control, it seems, would rest in Toronto. The Senate banking and commerce committee was told that the purpose of the bank would be to help finance operations in western Canada and to aid small businessmen in western Canada. It was even suggested the company would build a couple of branch offices in Alberta and, I think, in one or two of the other western provinces.
This house is fully aware that many small businessmen are not able to do their banking in the larger cities. As one who represents a rural area outside Calgary I was particularly interested to learn whether this bank proposed to make any effort to aid the people I represent. I came to the conclusion after reading the report of the Senate committee, that the bank was simply masquerading under
Private Bills
the name of "The Bank of Western Canada"- that control, and probably its interests, would lie in Toronto and in eastern Canada. It is for this reason I hesitate to see the bill pass readily this afternoon without anything further being said about it. I certainly hope it will be referred to the banking and commerce committee of the House of Commons so that we can take another close look at the distribution of shares. I am told that since this matter came before the Senate committee on banking and commerce there has been a reshuffling of the ownership of these shares.
The company is asking this parliament for a great privilege. It is asking for a charter to operate a bank in Canada. This is a monopoly given to only a few, and while I support the principle that there should be more banks operating in Canada under federal charter I am somewhat dubious concerning this particular bank because of the attempt to masquerade under the name of "The Bank of Western Canada". If they had called it "The Bank of Toronto" I might have been less suspicious. Perhaps that name would have involved duplication. But why did they not choose another name? Perhaps they could have called it the "Bank of Eastern Canada". It would I think have been more appropriate for this group, and I would see less reason for hesitating about granting this charter. A person who tries to masquerade under a false name is always the object of some suspicion, and perhaps that is why I am suspicious of this particular company asking us to grant them a charter to operate under the Bank Act, together with other banks.
As I say, they are asking us for a valuable monopoly and we have every right to inquire closely into the ownership of this company to find out whether it will be Canadian and whether it will remain in Canadian hands. I should like to see the ownership in as many hands as possible rather than in only a few hands. From the reports of the Senate committee it appears that by and large three people will have a controlling interest in this venture. I have no objection to ownership by three people, but I wish it were 300. We would then have more people able to share in the benefits of the monopoly. This house should always concern itself greatly about the granting of monopolies. Monopolies give tremendous power to the companies benefiting by them.
I will end by saying that I wish the mover of this bill would say that it is proposed to refer it to the standing committee of the House of Commons on banking and commerce for further examination.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on Bill No. S-6, to comment more particularly on some of the reasons why those large companies enjoy very special privileges which any other company is unable to get.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate on this bill, I would like to make a few observations on the Canadian banking system, especially on the control which financial interests can exercise on the economy of the country and also, directly, on the personal life of every Canadian citizen, depending on the good will of those gentlemen, the bank managers, who control our lives by the decisions they make.
It should be noted that those bank managers often meet and are quite in agreement when they attend board meetings of electric power, textile, paper, railways, tobacco or wheat trusts, to mention only those and, of course, they are all members of the ultrasecret Canadian bankers association. It is there that finance and the economy of trade and industry are controlled; it is there that low salaries and high prices are established.
There are eight banks in Canada and the four most powerful control 80 per cent of all Canadian business. All the branches, 5,600 of them, with ramifications throughout Canada, are the faithful and affiliated skimmers which reap everywhere, for the benefit of the central bank, the outcome of the people's labours.
The cause of every economic crisis, war and sudden change of capital is to be found there, rather than in the so-called deficiencies of international trade. If bankers are so powerful, it is because they have the exclusive power to create money as they need it, while all other citizens of the country must

work to earn a living, and deprive themselves in order to save a little. They eventually get into debt with those institutions because even sovereign governments are under their yoke.
It is almost impossible for honest citizens to go up in the world of wealth because all millionaires made their money through flagrant and immoral injustices, company and bank acts which the governments use to give the directors of those institutions exclusive privileges, unmatched power to the disadvantage of the other institutions or individuals in the country, to the disadvantage of society and governments themselves.
The taxation system itself, as set up today by the governments and the municipalities, also favours the wealthy and the powerful to the disadvantage of the poor, the little fellow and the weak. Should not the governments, bodies of society to serve society, protect the weak as well as the strong?
Therefore, I ask all the very rich people, the small and big capitalists in 1964, to assess to what extent they have been, in some way, exceptionally favoured by those three major discriminatory institutions of modem society, the Bank Act, the company legislation and the fiscal legislation.
It will appear abundantly clear to the millionaires, the wealthy and the well-off people that their wealth was derived more or less from those three major injustices; it is their responsibility, therefore, to contribute, according to their means, to the readjustment of society, in order to restore a proper balance on the social, national, personal and family plan.
And you, the poor and underprivileged Canadians, do not think that this money will be given to you for nothing. Society will just allow you to take advantage, through a social readjustment, of the share you were unfairly deprived of in the past.
It is to be noted that banks are sound and good as well as useful and necessary institutions, but one must also recognize that one of the laws on bank credit constitutes one of the three great legal injustices of modern times. We do not have to demolish everything but to correct and better those institutions. Reforms are necessary if those institutions are to be adapted to the new conditions which they have themselves created, but until a competent authority puts the house in order, it is still better to respect the existing disorder than create complete disorder by revolt and anarchy.

For instance, an application for the setting up of a provincial bank has been rejected by the Senate.
The Senate has turned down a bill respecting a provincial bank and it wants to approve a bill sponsored by a few private individuals. The Senate is ready to give a charter to individuals, to private institutions, but it denies it to a province. A province deserves as much consideration as a few individuals-
Order. May I draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that he cannot refer, as he does at the present time, to procedures of the other house.

Far be it from me to make bitter criticism to appeal to the passions of the people. I merely wish to examine the facts of which the people are unaware and to explain what should be and what the people want. Studies improve one's mind, expands one's horizons and add to one's stature. To be practical, we will indicate a logical, social and legal way of carrying out such a reform in an orderly and peaceful fashion.
Consequently, I take the liberty of saying that the banks put out credit money and cheque money which are used by the people as instruments of exchange just as if they were legal tender. In other words, they are nothing but legalized bogus money. The banks have the power to increase the money supply by creating credit money.
They lend to themselves large amounts they create out of nothing and that is where they hold an advantage over those who must save to accumulate capital.
Pope Pius XI was clearsighted. Did he not say in an encyclical:
What strikes us at the present time is the tremendous and discretionary power in the hands of a small number of individuals, this power is especially formidable among those who are the absolute masters of money, controlling credit according to their discretion.
They are infusing blood in the economic system which rests in their hands so that without their consent nobody could survive. The strongest alone still stand, that is the most aggressive and unscrupulous ones.
Therefore, we stated our reform proposals on many occasions and we repeat them: take away from the banks the issuance of credit money and the sovereign authority shall resume its role concerning the issuance of money, of all the money required for trade.
The real money based on the large production of Canada, plentiful, based on man,

on his trading requirements and on his production capacities. We must therefore restore justice, make a distribution of ill-gotten gains and then set up an economic system to preserve justice and maintain a balance between social classes for the general welfare of mankind.
I am a member of the parliament of Canada in Ottawa. What does that mean?
In my riding of Compton-Frontenac, I am the representative of 22,000 voters, and of the 45,000 citizens who actually live in my riding.
To live, those 45,000 citizens need money every day, every month, every year.
That money that citizens of my riding need so badly is not manufactured in my riding, by any citizen of my riding nor in any other riding. In my riding the citizens produce all kinds of commodities for other citizens of the community; they make furniture, cheese, houses, churches, schools, roads, but no one manufactures money.
All across the land seven million citizens manufacture all kinds of things required by human people for their living in Canada, but no one can manufacture the money that all citizens need so badly to purchase the goods and services required for their subsistence.
The issuing of money is reserved to the Bank of Canada, as regards notes in circulation, which total approximately $2.2 billion, and since that amount cannot meet the circulation requirements and the need for exchange on the part of the people, private banks have been authorized to create some sort of credit money, script money, bookkeeping money, accounting money, money which cannot be seen with the naked eye, a permission which those private banks have used to the extent of over $17 billion, and that is eight times more money than the Bank of Canada supplies.
The result is that our eight private banks, taking advantage of this exclusive privilege to create money and all forms of capital, have seen their directors become board members of the 800 largest companies on the stock market.
That is why this kind of business may tempt newcomers, that is why we are being faced with applications for three new banks in Canada.
Must we accept or must we reject those three applications? Are we going to allow an increase in the number of companies and banks which are taking unfair advantage of the public through those money-making

I particularly say that because there has been a subsequent poll introduced in this debate which was carried out by Gruneau Research Limited. I presume this poll took place some time during the month of July. The results of this poll were published in the Victoria Daily Colonist on August 6 and indicated that this was a survey of some
2.000	people across the country. By rough and ready reckoning, Mr. Speaker, that would appear to be about 200 people per province. It indicates that in the province of British Columbia the red ensign is favoured by 32.1 per cent, that the maple leaf flag is favoured by 29.9 per cent and another flag by 15.8 per cent. There were 17.9 per cent who did not care and 4.3 per cent who did not know. I would suggest the comparison between 32 per cent in favour of the red ensign and approximately 30 per cent in favour of the maple
Canadian Flag
leaf design is not bad when one considers the new proposed flag had only been known to the public for, if I may refer to it as a sailor, a dogwatch. I think the results of this poll indicate that this flag it catching on across the country and will grow in favour once people become aware of its symbolism.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to waste much time in this regard but before I leave this question of who is guiding me I should like to point out one further fact, and this is something that has had some effect upon me, I must say. I find that the man who represented the Conservative party in the last election and who ran against me has placed his views in respect of the flag on record in a Victoria newspaper. He did so shortly after the government's proposal was made public. Mr. Chairman said:
Many thousands of flag designs have been suggested over the past years. If this design has been deemed best, it should be adopted.
The red ensign has been accepted as the official flag for some time now, and for most of that time all political parties have been demanding a new one that would be distinctly Canadian.
Those who insist on a plebiscite to decide the issue are showing irresponsibility. It has been a major election platform of all major Canadian political parties for some years to adopt a new Canadian flag-surely they must represent a majority of the Canadian people.
There has never been a better time to finalize the issue than on the eve of Canada's centenary. And Mr. Pearson, heading a minority government, cannot be criticized for trying to push it through wantonly.
Mr. Speaker, that is all I have to say in respect of the poll question and now wish to make one or two remarks about letters that have been received. The letters I have received have not been very great in quantity and I find that to be somewhat surprising, coming as I do from Victoria where people have, as I have said before, very great affection for the union jack and for the red ensign. I would have thought that if anything would have aroused public reaction for or against, it would have been the last paragraph of my letter to the newspaper of June 10 which was referred to by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) this afternoon because, having explained what my own stand was to be on the flag, I said in that paragraph:
Not all of these have been easy decisions to make, but I was sent to parliament to consider all aspects of proposed legislation and then to vote on behalf of all the people of Victoria. Bearing in mind both the present and the future of Canada, I firmly believe the moves I have outlined are both right and responsible, and I hope Victorians generally will agree.
That letter appeared in the weekly and daily newspapers in Victoria and as a result

I had something less than a flood of letters. Altogether since this issue came forward I have had considerably less than 200 letters or communications of one sort or another on the flag issue. Since June 10, when my letter was published in the newspaper, I do not think I have had more than 50 letters. These have by no means all been unfavourable, although I am not going to try to pretend they have all been favourable either. We know this is not an easy matter to decide. I am just pointing out the intensity of public interest and I am trying to show that as far as I can establish we have heard on this matter from considerably fewer than 5 per cent of the people who live in my riding, even if we assume that almost all of those who wrote to the newspaper and sent in their ballots come from Victoria-which they do not, of course, bearing in mind once again the wide distribution of this newspaper.
I should like to leave that point for a moment and go on to another matter which was brought up by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) this afternoon when he claimed that the three maple leaves are a Liberal symbol. I just cannot accept that. I would like to pose these questions to the house. First of all, is it because it was a Liberal symbol that King George V in 1921 at the time of the government of Sir Robert Borden had the three maple leaves designated as the national emblem of Canada and incorporated these same three conjoined maple leaves in the coat of arms of Canada? I do not think so. Is it because it was a Liberal symbol that the former prime minister, now Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), had three maple leaves placed on the bumper of his official car? Is it because it is a Liberal symbol that Her Majesty the Queen had the three maple leaves conjoined placed in a position of honour on her royal standard as Queen of Canada? I just do not believe so.
All these uses were made of this symbol because three conjoined maple leaves on a white background mean Canada. In my view, Mr. Speaker, it is because these three maple leaves are above politics, because they are highly respected and, I may dare to say, because they are a noble symbol that I personally find it very easy to support the flag motion, remembering all the time that the second part of the resolution calls for the retention of the union jack as the commonwealth flag. I remind hon. members that the red maple leaf, sometimes one and sometimes three, was used on the funnels of Canadian ships during world war II to distinguish 
them from British and Australian warships. I remember that in my own experience. I am told that today on Cyprus the three maple leaves are being painted and appear on the rocks anywhere near where Canadian soldiers are stationed. I am also told that when the defence committee visited the Atlantic coast the other day these symbols were appearing, perhaps unobtrusively but nevertheless appearing, in various spots down below in the engine rooms and boiler rooms and so forth of the ships in the Atlantic fleet.
A single maple leaf.

So I think it can be said without any fear of contradiction that the three red maple leaves also have a very firm place in the affections of our countrymen.
I want to skip over very quickly the matter of a plebiscite. My views on the plebiscite are somewhat the same as those of the mother of parliaments, where in the whole of the life of the parliament of the United Kingdom there has never been a plebiscite. We have had our own rather dismal experience here in Canada where we have had two plebiscites, I believe, neither of which was acted upon and neither of which seemed to solve anything. So this only confirms my attitude toward a plebiscite.
Deciding on a flag is a tough decision. If it were not, I suggest it is a decision which would have been made many years ago. But surely making tough decisions is our job in parliament. That is surely what we were sent here for. We cannot duck our duty by referring this matter to a committee or to the forum of public opinion in a plebiscite. I suggest that we are the biggest, most powerful and most expensive committee there is and if we cannot solve this matter I venture to say that certainly no committee can.
I should like to say something about another reason why I think this matter cannot be referred to a committee. Having regard to the length of time that this matter has been discussed in the house and with all the various ramifications and the stories we have heard about one flag or another, I believe that we ourselves are becoming somewhat confused, but we must think of how confused the public must be on this issue. I should like to point out some aspects of this confusion that have become apparent to me in my investigations, but as I will not have time to finish my address if I give them all I will confine my remarks merely to one. We have been told a lot about the red ensign and told in all sincerity, I know, of how it has been the flag

under which Canadians have fought and died for a number of years, but particularly in the second world war. In my own experience I know that as far as the navy is concerned we saw little of the red ensign, unless a sailor happened to be serving in the merchant navy on a defensively equipped merchant ship. We flew the white ensign. We all know the air force flag which, incidentally, has the R.C.A.F. roundel with a maple leaf in the centre.
When it comes to the army I am on rather dangerous ground, so I took the trouble the other day to visit the national war museum. There I found some relics of Dieppe. I know there are hon. members in this house who were present on that occasion and I suppose that of all the Canadian feats of arms this is one that is remembered best as being a part of Canada. I saw hanging in our Canadian national war museum a flag. Under that flag there was this inscription:
This flag was captured by the enemy during the second Canadian division raid on Dieppe, August 19, 1942.
For nearly two years it hung, a prized trophy on the wall in the office of a German colonel there, and was then packed for shipment to Germany.
The fine loyalty of a French woman prevented this, however,
Madame Jovene, 8 rue Guerrier, Dieppe, extracted it from its packing case and concealed it until, a month later on September 1, 1944, the same second Canadian division recaptured Dieppe, when she proudly returned it to its rightful owners.
This flag, Mr. Speaker, was the union jack. I see my time is running out, but I am almost finished. Our job in this house is to legislate for Canada. Our particular problem at the moment is Canadian unity. I am looking, myself, for the kind of unity we have never had in this country. I hope that this flag will help. As I said before, we can resolve this issue and I, for one, am not unhopeful of the future. If we do not solve the difficulties of our time in our generation, then perhaps if we prepare the ground properly our young people will do so.
I do want to say one more thing, Mr. Speaker. Some reference was made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) to the fact that he was worried about the division this flag debate is causing within the country. He is frightened by the reaction. He put on the record a letter containing some reference to our fellow Canadians of French speaking origin. I will not dignify it by repeating it and having it placed in Hansard twice. He mentioned the fact a great number of Canadians are not going to accept this flag. Well, if he gets that reaction, it is not the one I get.

"No editorial comment from The Leader-

It matters to me.

These are his figures, not mine.
-about nine to one. (If you don't believe that, ask people; first ascertaining that they are Canadians.)

I would like to say, incidentally, that I agree with the views which my fellow member, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) expressed this afternoon, when he said that our discussions in this house do not always find their true explanation over the mass media.
I agree still more with him when he says that the C.B.C., in order to speak only of one of those mass media, does not serve the people well.
Order.

That young man told me that what he read in Hansard was entirely different from what he heard on the C.B.C. newscasts and read in some newspapers.
At the beginning of my remarks, I congratulated my colleagues on this side of the house for the moderate terms they use to air their views. Most of my Anglo-Saxon colleagues in the house did not hide the fact that their constituents support the red ensign and that they feel it is their duty to speak as they do.
I must say that I have a lot of admiration and respect for them, for the courage they have shown in giving to the house the views and aspirations of their constituents, which unfortunately is not the case for the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) who said that although she represents a riding which favours the Canadian red ensign, she will not take her constituents' aspirations and views into account when she casts her vote.

On the contrary, all the members who have spoken on this side of the house displayed a great understanding and also stated their willingness to accept a compromise that would be reasonable for all parties concerned, so as to settle the ticklish problem concerning the national flag issue or rather the national flags, since we are talking about adopting two flags.
I said a while ago that I was rising in order to do my duty towards my constituents. I wish at the outset to state clearly the stand I must take as regards the Canadian flag, while basing myself on my constituents' aspirations and desires.
I must say that the freedom we are enjoying in our party also enables me to state that I am in favour of a national distinctive flag.
On this side of the house, our hands are not already tied by party discipline. We can voice our opinions as we please. We have the right and are free to vote as we see fit, and we also have the right to make our views known in whatever way we choose.

I regret that our hon. friends opposite do not enjoy that same freedom. If I am not mistaken, that should explain why the hon. members from the province of Quebec are not taking part in this debate. On those occasions when they did speak, they limited themselves to bitter remarks-

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I should like to remind the hon. member that the reason we, on this side of the house, are not saying anything on the flag issue is that our position is quite clear. We are definitely in favour of a distinctive flag and against a second flag.

A few moments ago, I said I was in favour of a distinctive flag. I have been careful not to say that I have taken a fancy to the three maple leaf flag but I am even more revolted with the way this flag was submitted to us.
Taking neither the house nor his cabinet into his confidence, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) went to Winnipeg to make his well known proposal. Even worse, when he came back from western Canada he walked into the house and said: "I have chosen a flag and I ask you to endorse it. A refusal on your part will be considered as a vote of non-confidence." Afterwards, he ordered his followers to toe the party line.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that is a dictatorial way of introducing such an important resolution which has raised such a controversy that the country is now on the verge of splitting up over the issue.
If, at least, we had been warned one way or the other, in the speech from the throne, that we would be called upon to choose a national flag this session, we would have no reason to complain since we would have known what was coming. However, there was nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that this topic would be discussed in the course of this session.
Members on the government side claim that this legislation is being introduced to fulfil an electoral pledge. What about the other promises concerning issues just as important if not more so than the national flag?
For instance, I remember that during the last election campaign the Liberals promised full employment.
But, has any action been taken to find jobs for the 105,000 unemployed in the province of Quebec?
Among other election promises, there was the appointment of a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada in order to help eastern farmers. There was also the adoption of a labour code and the establishment of a minimum salary of $1.25 per hour. There was also the institution of a portable pension

plan. All those promises have yet to be fulfilled. I could mention many other promises, but I will refrain from doing so.
For what purpose, then, was this project of a Canadian flag brought out of the blue? For a very simple purpose, Mr. Speaker. Conscious of its inertia, the government wanted to hide behind this resolution its weaknesses, its indecision and its inability to face up to its responsibilities.
This could have been overlooked if the Prime Minister had not raised the question of non-confidence. But after having done so is it at all conceivable that hon. members opposite would not fulfil their obligations toward their party? I cannot see it at all.
Mr. Speaker, it must be recognized that we are faced with a problem threatening national unity, and to substantiate my allegation, I wish to quote from a few newspaper articles which clearly prove that this legislation has given rise to serious concerns in various quarters.
I have here an article signed by Mr. Guy Cormier and published in La Presse on May 19, 1964 and entitled:
A flag or an expedient?
Having promised a flag to Canadians, Mr. Pearson is unfurling it today before an astonished or indifferent Canada.
Confused and irritated, judging by the noisy reactions to his speech delivered before the Canadian Legion in Winnipeg. Those who are unconcerned refrain from showing their feelings, as is only natural when anything is obtained after an unreasonable waiting period. A distinctive Canadian flag has been requested for a long time in the province of Quebec-
A little further on, the editor says:
The government leader proposes the maple leaf in the name of unity. One can hardly find another great virtue in the name of which he could push his proposal forward. Such unity is a wish, it is not a reality. It is less than ever a reality. Things first come into existence, then the symbols they represent are created. Mr. Pearson is proceeding by means of artificial insemination.
In its issue of May 21, 1964, the newspaper La Presse published the following article under the byline of Gerard Pelletier.
A symbol, yes, but of what?
Nobody will be led to believe that the flag issue is a major problem in Canadian polities. It is a matter which was left to deteriorate instead of being settled; it is only a matter of symbols and, whatever the solution which is adopted, this action by itself will have but little effect on our Canadian life.
That is a further proof, Mr. Speaker, that there are other and more urgent problems which have been tackled this session.

Further on, Mr. Pelletier says:
In fact, claim his supporters, it is not so much a flag that Mr. Pearson is seeking; it is a majority.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt whatsoever in my mind that this flag question was brought forward merely for electoral purposes. According to the various polls carried out in the name of the government, if the results had been as anticipated, you and I, Mr. Speaker, would not be here today, we would be in the midst of an election campaign. Now, Mr. Pearson, the Prime Minister of this country, wants to give his flag to Canada, and he even claims that it is urgent.
In fact, it has been urgent for a long time, and Mr. Pearson never seemed to be too much concerned with that problem in the past.

Concerning Mr. Pearson's proposed flag which is seemingly an enlarged copy of the latest postage stamp issued in the country, it does not seem to have been well received.

To summarize, if the French speaking population cannot get satisfaction with a standard likely to inspire its patriotism, it will approach with more

Mr. Speaker, I do possess the ability to understand speeches in both languages. I am sure I understand English better than that hon. member understands

French. I am able to follow what hon. members are saying in both languages, and I am proud to say so. The remark made by the hon. member just points out his ignorance.

I am going to prove it, because I have here a sheet from the newspaper Le Clairon of St. Hyacinthe, in which the Liberal party published on April 4, 1963, that is, during the election campaign, the following advertisement:
