Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to rise in the house on this occasion. I should first like to congratulate the many fine speakers who have spoken in this house in respect
Canadian Flag
of the subamendment. I certainly do not agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) when he refers to these speeches as part of a filibuster. I do agree with the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) when he said that he believed, rightly or wrongly, that everyone who has taken part in this debate has done so with sincerity and integrity. I believe these people represent the constituents for whom they have spoken. I do not agree with the unreasonable statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have sat throughout this debate and listened to some very fine and educational remarks in reference to this subamendment.
Mr. Speaker, last week I was invited to participate in a very wonderful ceremony in my constituency. This ceremony was in fact the official opening of a powwow on the Thunderchild Indian reservation. I was amazed at what took place during this ceremony, and a great deal went through my mind when I saw the R.C.M.P. officers dressed in their scarlet tunics standing at attention, along with these native Canadians, during the raising of the red ensign. I remembered at that time that here in parliament we were trying to destroy that symbol which these people have accepted so graciously. This fact caused me to do a lot of thinking. I have thought since I arrived back in the House of Commons that it was too bad that some of those members on the opposite side were not able to take part in that ceremony and witness how these people prize the red ensign. When I stood there and heard the national anthem sung in the Cree language I could not help but think of what was going on in parliament.
In the subamendment the first question set forth is: "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign"? We have many reasons to be in favour of the Canadian red ensign when we look back and think of what it has meant to us down through the years. However, one thing I have noted in the debate and which I have admired is that every speaker who has taken part on this side has said he is quite in agreement with some modifications being made to the red ensign if necessary to create unity in this great country. I have been very happy to see this attitude and I was also pleased with the proposal that the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), placed before the house and the government. I fail to see how the government could not accept such a proposal. There was no mention of the flag question in the speech from the throne

Canadian Flag
at the commencement of this session of parliament and I cannot understand why the flag resolution could not be withdrawn at this time in favour of the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
Since the government took office it has withdrawn much of the legislation it has put before the house, and I think it would not hurt the government to accept the fact once again that they have made a blunder and to withdraw the resolution they have placed on the order paper, which is so unnecessary at this time having in mind all the disunity that the government has already created with the B and B gang. Without a doubt I think they should withdraw the resolution, admit that once again they have taken off in the wrong direction and come forward with a proposal for a committee as suggested by the two members to whom I have referred. The hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) admitted as much yesterday and more Liberals should have been in the house to listen to the very fine speech he made. As found on page 7033 of Hansard he said:
We on this side have wondered how it is that so many people in Canada are staunchly entrenched behind the red ensign, a fact we did not expect-
He admits this is so, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure that as time goes on it will be found that there are a great many more people who are behind the red ensign. I recall that when I went home to my constituency on week ends at the time this matter first came up for debate people were very lukewarm and not much concerned about the flag debate or a change in the flag. In many cases they said to me: Have you fellows got nothing else to do down there but debate the flag? However, I have noticed lately that it is a different story. They come and pat me on the back and say: "Don't you fellows give in with respect to this very rude thing that the government is trying to do to this country". In my constituency I have people from every ethnic group in Europe. I might say I am proud of the French blood in my veins and the Irish blood also, but I am sure if my late mother and father were here they would be happy with the stand I am taking. My father was reared in Quebec before going to western Canada, and we were very happy to live under the red ensign. As I have said, however, we would be perfectly willing to accept some modification to show the great traditions of the founding races of this nation.
In my constituency there are many people who came from the province of Quebec and I have not received one letter opposing the

red ensign as our national flag. I have people from every ethnic group in Europe in my constituency and I have not received one letter or heard one word from them opposing the red ensign. I have not received a single letter supporting the three maple leaves flag. I think it is a shame that this flag should be forced on the people at this time. I disagree with many who talk about the great expense this debate and a plebiscite would be to the country and all the tommyrot they utter in an attempt to force the opposition to give up trying to discharge its responsibility. Members of parliament are paid by the year as are the staff. The only additional cost is the stenographic staff. I say that we have our democratic rights and that if we want to stand up for the people we represent we have no other alternative but to oppose this ridiculous proposal, and we must do so.
Not having referred to the flag question in the speech from the throne I think that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) acted very unjustly when he appeared as guest speaker before that great body, the Canadian Legion and told them that this flag would be the flag whether they liked it or not. He was invited there as the guest speaker but he took advantage of the time and the opportunity to make a political speech and to tell them that this would be the flag whether they liked it or not. I think the Legion had no alternative but to boo and jeer him. He was invited there as a guest speaker but he took the opportunity to make a political speech and to try to unfurl his flag before that great organization whose members have done so much in two world wars and who are solidly behind the Canadian red ensign. I think this was a disgrace.
Many have seen the cartoons discrediting this great organization, the Canadian Legion, by implying that only the drunks in the Legion were supporting the red ensign. I think this is a shame. Many people in my constituency have not written letters but have come to me and said: If there is a majority in favour of this flag why do you fellows not go along with it? I say that these are people who would give up their flag and country for a political party, and in my opinion that is a shame. I do not rate very highly any group of people who will give up their flag, their country and their traditions for a political party.
The second question in the subamendment is: "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?"

I think I have covered that point. It has been definitely shown that we in this party are willing to go along with certain changes in the red ensign to show distinctly the heritages of the two founding races. I think this is very important. I for one would hate to see the union jack removed from any distinctive Canadian flag. I believe it has a place "there and I think we have every right to ask that it be left there. But I would not oppose adding the fleur-de-lis or any other symbol. There are many ways in which this could be done.
I support strongly the proposal made by the hon. member for Oxford and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle but I also have a proposal I should like the government to consider. I suggest that the provinces should be brought into the picture. Let their representatives have a say as to what should be the Canadian flag. I think this is very Important, Mr. Speaker, because when I go from one province to another across this *country I do not want to find each one with a different symbol. I think this would be a shame. I would go along with the proposal for a committee to be set up on which each province would have representation and have an opportunity to voice its opinion. I am sure we have men and women who are qualified to be members of such a committee. I am sure this committee would come out with a flag of which we could all be proud, and I am *sure that the heritage of the two founding races would be represented on such a flag. Then we could go from one province to another saying, this is our Canadian flag.
You go across the border to the south and go from one state to another and you will not find a different flag. We should have our own, distinctive Canadian flag. I think we should be broadminded enough to take this question out of politics by setting up a committee upon which all provinces would be represented. This committee would come out with a flag of which we could all be proud. We will never arrive at a decision in the House of Commons. We are, I suppose, trying to bring politics into this question of arriving at a distinctive Canadian flag. This reminds me of a cartoon I saw recently in one of the weekly newspapers. A tourist was standing looking up at two flags, one was the Esso sign and the other was the three maple leaf design. He said, "Just which one is your distinctive Canadian flag?" This is the pre-*dicament in which we find ourselves. We are
Canadian Flag
well aware of the fact that very few provinces are going to accept the three maple leaf design.
When I return to western Canada and go through the cities I find that people realize something is going to be taken away from them which they have held dear and you can see more ensigns flying than ever in the history of our country. We should pull ourselves together. The leaders should reach agreement to take this resolution out of the Commons at this stage, set up a committee jointly with the provinces and bring in a flag of which we can all be proud. We were told in the early stages of this flag controversy that there was going to be a free vote. How quickly that wilted away. There will be no free vote.
We recall that there were not supposed to be two flags at the start. However, Joey Smallwood was not satisfied and said he was going to fly the union jack in Newfoundland. Then they introduced the union jack as a second flag. This is ridiculous. Surely, we can get down to business here and bring in a truly Canadian flag of which we can all be proud, and give all the provinces a chance to say that they were able to express their views on this flag. I do not know why the flag question was introduced at this time because there was no mention of it in the speech from the throne.
One of the questions referred to in the subamendment is: Are you in favour of the three maple leaves? I think I have made it very clear where I stand on the three maple leaves. We already have them on the red ensign. I have always respected the maple leaf, even though it does not grow in my constituency. I have always respected it because it has been our symbol as long as I can remember. However, I go along with the statement made by her worship the mayor of Ottawa, that this flag looks like three dead maple leaves on a field of surrender. This is what it looked like to me. I am sure a great many members sitting across the way feel the same way because I have heard some of them express their opinions on this flag.
Then, the fourth question in the subamendment is: Are you in favour of a one maple leaf flag? The one maple leaf flag does not mean any more to me than the three maple leaf flag. If something were added in the flag such as a beaver, a sheaf of wheat, a buffalo or even a good Hereford bull, that would mean more to me. These are some of my views on this subject. As I pointed out, the maple leaf does not grow in my constituency. I am sure, as many members of parliament

Canadian Flag
will agree, we have many designers in this country and if we had a committee on which all the provinces of Canada were represented, we would have no difficulty in arriving at a distinctive flag.
I do not go along with those people, Mr. Speaker, who are saying how terrible it is that we are holding up parliament. We are not holding up parliament. We are representing constituencies and we have to exercise our democratic rights. We are well aware of the fact that if this three maple leaf flag is adopted we will have it for a long time. This is the reason people here are fighting this issue. They want justice and that is all these people want. They are not filibustering. They are speaking up for their democratic rights and they have a right to be heard.
I do not blame the Prime Minister alone for this situation. I blame hon. members sitting opposite for allowing this flag question to be introduced. What were they doing in caucus when they allowed this measure to be brought forward? They talk about a free vote, but they have no free vote. I blame those who are sitting on the benches opposite for not voicing their opinions, and allowing this matter to come before parliament. They should have spoken up instead of acting like a bunch of trained seals. I hope the Prime Minister of this country, that great Nobel prize winner, will take hold of this thing and remove it from the House of Commons. He would be making another retreat but he has made so many now that one more will not hurt. He should set up a committee and let us get on with some of the other business this government promised the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate this evening for two reasons. I feel I have an obligation, on behalf of the people I represent in the House of Commons, to place before this house some of the views that have been indicated to me by letter and otherwise. The second reason is that I think we have reached a stage in this debate when some of us at least should be discussing ways and means or possibilities of reaching an agreement on this resolution and the amendments to it.
I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) (Mr. Groos) earlier this evening because I am faced with a situation similar to that which he described. I have received letters, telegrams and petitions from the people I represent expressing a wide variety of viewpoints on this issue. I wish to say, also, that I am in sympathy to

some extent with the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu) who has just resumed his seat when he says we should take political partisanship out of the debate on a flag for Canada.
Before this can be done, however, there are one or two essential concessions which must be made. One of these, in my opinion, is that there should be a declaration by the leaders of all parties in this house on behalf of their followers that there will be a completely free vote. As I said, I think I have an obligation to present to this house some of the expressions of opinion I have received. I have gone over these communications very carefully-there are dozens, perhaps hundreds of them- and I think the five or six from which I intend to quote are representative of the whole of the correspondence I have received. First, I have a letter from Taber from which I wish to read an extract. It says:
I hope you will be able to support the government with your vote on the flag issue. I am not particularly concerned about the design chosen but I am, like most of those with whom I have talked, in favour of a distinctive flag for Canada free of British or French symbols.
I am a British ex-serviceman of the second world war and a member of the Canadian Legion. The official attitude of the Legion X consider ill-founded.
My Legion branch will be informed of the contents of this letter.
Well, here is an ex-serviceman and a member of the Legion who has clearly stated his position. He is in favour of a flag for Canada which does not carry the symbols of any other country. Here is another letter:
Please be advised that a telegram has been sent to the Prime Minister of Canada which reads as follows-that the Medicine Hat junior chamber of commerce has gone on record as favouring the flag chosen by the government of Canada as the national flag of Canada.
I was not at this meeting when the resolution was passed by the junior chamber of commerce, but I understand there was a sharp division of opinion during the course of the debate and that the motion barely passed by a very small majority.
Here is another letter:
As one of your constituents I would like to register a strong protest on the design of the projected flag as proposed by Prime Minister Pearson.
While personally I would prefer the red ensign because it is the flag for which our boys fought and died, however, I would not mind a flag with one maple leaf (green or multicoloured on a red background).

This is a letter which indicates that the writer is not in favour of the design suggested in the motion. The writer is not particularly adamant about retaining the red ensign, either. So here we have another point of view. Here is a further letter:
I hope I am not too late to let you know of my very strong feelings on the red ensign.
As far as my family, relatives and friends are concerned, we believe we have a distinctive Canadian flag and want no tampering with it in any way, shape or form.
I plead with you to vote against Lester Pearson's pennant and if it means another election that is a small matter in comparison.
I think this represents a somewhat extreme position. Nevertheless, it is an opinion held by some of my constituents.
I also have a letter here from the I.O.D.E. of Medicine Hat saying:
We wish to inform you that, we of the municipal chapter I.O.D.E., are in favour of the red ensign being upheld as the national flag of Canada.
So it goes. Here is another:
Dear Mr. Olson,
In your work as our representative in parliament, it may help you to know how some of us feel and think on certain issues.
The ensign with its union jack, and the Canadian coat of arms on a red background holds a great deal of meaning to me.
Having worked with girl guides of Canada for many years, I have learned the legends of the patron saints. These men were not national heroes but dedicated Christians. It is this spiritual value that is uplifting and inspiring.
When I see the maple leaf, there is no special feeling involved except that we used to do a drill and sing the fine song in school; and a special folk dance I know ends with "The Maple Leaf Forever". The leaf itself holds no spiritual inspiration.
And, finally:
As a resident of your constituency, I wish to express my opinion on the Canadian flag issue.
I feel it is very important to the future of our country that we have a flag which is truly a Canadian flag. I am in favour of a maple leaf design or whatever symbol, that is a "Canadian" one, is adopted.
Both the fleur-de-lis and the union jack have flown over our soil in the past. The red ensign I feel is also a flag of the past. It is an adaptation of the flag of another country. It cannot any longer be a true symbol of a country that is populated by peoples of such varied and diverse cultural backgrounds. New Canadians arrive daily in our country. Let them be able to identify with a symbol that is truly Canadian. Canada certainly lacks national unity and sometimes I think a strong national feeling. Our feelings are either too "British" or too "American". Let us hope that a new Canadian flag will set us going as a strong united people with a strong national feeling for our great and wonderful country.
I may say, also, that all the Royal Canadian Legion branches in my constituency, sent me letters or telegrams expressing their
Canadian Flag
desire that Canada should retain the red ensign. But the point I am trying to make in reading these examples of correspondence is that in my constituency there is support for the retention of the red ensign, support for a flag with the three maple leaves combined on one stem and an expression of support for a single maple leaf design. This places a member in a position in which it is impossible for him to vote on the subamendment, or on the amendment, or on the main motion, and represent all his people. I think one has to consider some of the alternatives. I wish to quote an editorial which appeared in the Medicine Hat News of May 14. It says this:
There should be no nonsense about voting along party lines in parliament when the government brings in its design for a national flag.
This was written prior to the introduction of the resolution.
This is not a matter which should be decided along party lines.
Prime Minister Pearson hinted that this may be the case when he remarked in the Commons Tuesday that "when the time comes to subject the decision of the government to the House of Commons, I would hope that every member of the house would vote as his conscience dictates and that there would be no question of confidence or non-confidence in a party sense."
Mr. Pearson is quite right, but he should go further and declare this a "free vote". Partisan politics have no place in an issue such as this. Certainly not the type of politicking demonstrated by Mr. John Diefenbaker, Tuesday who, after hearing the Prime Minister's remarks, said "another retreat".
It is precisely this kind of petty politicking which should be avoided when the question of a national flag comes before the house.
Mr. Pearson is right, too, when he says the issue should not become one of confidence or nonconfidence in the government.
This is a matter for each member to vote on as an individual; a vote to be dictated by his constituents' wishes in so far as he knows them and his own conscience.
Let the issue be faced squarely and honestly with no taint of party politics.
Even tonight we heard the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu), a member of the Progressive Conservative party, suggest that partisan politics ought to be taken out of the decision with respect to this flag. I submit to you, sir, that there are three essential courses that must be followed if we are to avoid the difficulty that I can see down the road in this connection. First of all we must have a firm statement from the Prime Minister that when the vote comes on the subamendment, the amendment and the resolution, it will be a completely free vote. This vote should not be tied to anything except the choosing of a national flag for Canada.

Canadian Flag
By that I mean it should not be tied to the threat of an election; it should not be tied to some kind of compromise or concession with regard to anything else.
There has been a great deal of talk during this debate about the divisions in the country. This is beginning to sound a little hollow, because it seems to me that the longer this debate goes on, the more we are agitating those divisions rather than healing them, if they do exist. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as I have said, the first consideration must be a free vote without any consideration other than selecting a national flag for this country. I should like to quote from a special letter to the Prime Minister of Canada from the Canadian corps association. This letter is dated August 5, and the last paragraph says:
The flag issue as it stands now, is destroying the members of parliaments' democratic right as elected representatives to render a just decision, and similarly, if this subject is not settled by a plebiscite, the people of this country will be forced to vote for the candidate in their constituency who shares their flag views.
This is the important part, Mr. Speaker:
What a sorry group of M.P.s we might have if candidates' over-all ability is pushed out of focus by only their opinion on Canada's flag.
I think we have come to the stage in this debate when we must seek some kind of compromise, if you want to call it that. When two immovable positions are taken, you may ask yourself, compromise in regards to what? If the reasons for taking those positions are not quite comprehensible, then it is difficult to decide how you can compromise. I hope the introduction of this particular design for a distinctive flag for Canada was predicated only on the desire to have a national flag adopted by parliament, and nothing else. I say that, Mr. Speaker, because we hear rumours that some of the Liberal members may add to their stature or enhance their position, particularly in the province of Quebec, if they can go back to the people with this pennant and say, "We of a Liberal government introduced into parliament and passed a distinctive flag for Canada". But the other side of the two positions has also to be considered. If the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his followers are continuing this debate solely because they do not want this particular design and they want the red ensign to remain as Canada's national flag, that is also an honest position. But we hear rumours that there may be some enhancement of their political position in parts of the country as long as they keep this filibuster

going. I read one letter that indicates there is one person at least in my constituency who would welcome a general election on the flag issue. I want to say that I do not accept that position, Mr. Speaker. As I said, there are two sides to this question and I think we have to try honestly to find a compromise that will be accepted by both sides of the house. To do that, one thing is essential; that is, that every member or, if this is not possible, at least the spokesmen for every political party shall assume the responsibility of trying to obtain the acceptance of the design after it is passed, whatever it is, and will not attempt to use it as a political wrench in an election.
Hear, hear.

One other thing that I think is important, Mr. Speaker, now the debate has gone this far and we have found a hardening of positions on both sides of the issue, is that when the flag is adopted, it ought to be a flag of parliament. At the present time I think many members of this house, and most of the Canadian people, feel that the design explained in the resolution-that is, three red maple leaves conjoined, on a white background with blue borders-is in fact a Liberal design or that it is, as it has been referred to, Pearson's pennant. I believe that the government, in order to reach some kind of compromise, ought to accept an amendment to the design and that amendment should come from somewhere in the opposition, be it from the Conservatives or any one of the other parties. Then when the decision has been taken, it will not have been a Liberal design or a Pearson pennant railroaded through parliament by sheer weight of numbers in the vote.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the three suggestions I have made-they are not new suggestions; I am not suggesting they are-ought to be seriously considered by both sides and both sides should try to come together on this question; otherwise I can see that this debate is going to go on and on. I believe that the positions, while they have hardened considerably, will become even worse. Then, when the decision has been taken, there will be wide division in the country in regard to accepting that flag, if it is the one described on the order paper at the present time.
Our party has stated over and over again that we will have a free vote in so far as our members are concerned. We are free to vote as our conscience directs and dictates on all the amendments and the resolution itself. This is what the Prime Minister asked the members of the house to do back in

May; I think it was early in May but I am not sure of the exact date. It was approximately May 10. I think the time has come when he should give an undertaking on
behalf of the government that they recognize that this is the way out. I would not be particularly concerned if the flag debate went on for another week or ten days, in spite of the fact that it is interfering with some of the other business to which parliament could be attending. It is not an unimportant matter to me, however. I do not know what the count is now, but something like 70 to 75 members must have spoken. I think that the rest of the members of this house, the other 190 or so, should also have the opportunity to speak on this flag debate before it terminates. Of course, what is happening is that hen. members do not speak just once. Amendments and subamendments are moved which provide an opportunity for each member to speak more than once, and this certainly carries the suspicion of a filibuster.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that we have to reach some kind of agreement, whether it be called a compromise or anything else, so that we can in fact get on with this matter. As I have said, I think we must have a declaration that there is going to be a free vote for the members of all parties in this house. Second, there should be an indication that the government will be willing to accept an amendment from the opposition so that the flag chosen will be the flag of parliament. That matter can be worked out at a leaders' meeting so that a suitable amendment can be proposed and accepted. Following that, Mr. Speaker, the matter could come to a vote and every hon. member of this house should assume the responsibility of obtaining or trying to obtain the acceptance of his constituents of the design, whatever it is and whenever it passes.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

Throughout the hon. gentleman's remarks he constantly described a filibuster the sincere and honest efforts made by the Conservative opposition. Would he indicate to the house his opinion of what constitutes a filibuster?

Well, Mr. Speaker, the definition of a filibuster is available to any hon. member who cares to look in one of the good dictionaries on the table. My impression of a filibuster is that it is a deliberate attempt 20220-449
Canadian Flag
to continue a debate for the sake of having time lapse, regardless of whether or not there is anything new to say on the subject.

One further question, if I may. Would the hon. member not agree that the word "filibuster" has no place in the Canadian parliament because it is an American process whereby a man can speak for unlimited time and read into the record any amount of material, which can come from Sears-Roebuck or even a telephone directory. In this house, as I understand it, we can speak for only 40 minutes and our remarks must be relevant to the topic on hand. Would he not agree that this debate is far removed from a filibuster?

Well, Mr. Speaker, as I have said, I do not have a dictionary before me so I can only give the hon. member a vivid, literal definition of the word. Perhaps the manner in which a filibuster is carried on in Canada is somewhat different from the United States, but I would suggest that the connotation put on the word "filibuster" by most hon. members in this house, as well as most Canadians, is completely in accord with the definition which I tried to give a few minutes ago.
Would the hon. member-

speechtext: Is the hon. member rising to ask a question?

Would the hon. member permit another question. I wonder whether I could ask him exactly where he stands with respect to the resolution as it is, as opposed to the red ensign. He has read into the record letters both for and against the red ensign, but it appeared to me that he slithered along in the middle, a tactic for which his leader is well known. I do not want to imply that I have known the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) for this particular habit, but where does he stand?

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my speech I made it abundantly clear that I felt it was my obligation and my duty to put before this parliament a reasonably accurate expression of opinion on the part of the people I represent in the constituency of Medicine Hat. I have done that. Now, if immediately after having done so I am going to have to say, before I have listened to the balance of the debate, what position I am going to take in this matter, it seems to me that this precludes my having an open mind on the suggestions which may be put forward within the next few days.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood)

Canadian Flag
rising to ask a question of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson)?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. For the last 20 minutes he straddled the fence and, like most Social Crediters, spoke out of both sides of his mouth at the same time. Would he now tell us whether or not he supports the red ensign?

The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood) wanted to ask me a question. I do not think we should accept the preamble to his question, which was really a speech and he has already had an opportunity to make his speech. He asked me point blank whether or not I am in favour of the red ensign. I want to say to him and to all other members of this house that when I was elected to represent the people of Medicine Hat I did not have a firm opinion on every single issue which was going to come before this parliament.

The republican wants to know about the flag.

Is the republican talking over there again? Mr. Speaker, I must apologize for my inability to understand that language in which the hon. member speaks. I have been scolded before for this inability. Mr. Speaker, I am sure a review of tomorrow's Hansard will indicate that great assistance has been given toward the prolonging of this debate by hon. members on the other side of the house. In my own interpretation of a filibuster you could hardly say there is one going on here.
Nothing like the truth.

During the debate charges have been made. We run into charges every day that the Conservative party is delaying the business of the nation. This is a most ridiculous charge and nobody is more aware of how ridiculous it is than the government. Every member in this house, both on this side and the other side, knows that if the government so wishes, the legislation to face us at the beginning of the week can be anything but the flag resolution. They could bring forward the pension legislation, provided it was ready or they could bring forward any other legislation they wished. Nobody on this side of the house has any control at all over the legislation that the government wishes to present to the house. Any inference that the discussion of the flag is holding up the nation's business is only an excuse on the part of the goverment for their inability to prepare the business of the nation and place it before the house.
In this respect I might also refer to further words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) as found on page 6958 of Hansard:
May I say this to my hon. friend, that if a party is determined to prolong the debate there is very little that can be done by any group, regardless of whether it is in the minority or majority.
I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is trying to deny the responsibility of the government in presenting legislation to the house. I would also point out that he has referred to the government and his own party as a group. He calls them a group. There is no mention of the leadership of the party. Here I might draw a parallel with what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) once said about the party. You will recall his famous statement. The Liberal party has the platform and the program, and we think we have a leader. The Minister of Trade and

Commerce has not even gone as far as to recognize the fact there is a party or a leader. He now refers to them as a group.
He wants the leader's job.
That is true. We all suspect he has his own ambitions.
Get back on the track.

With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, I would ask that order be called. If the member insists on hollering "get back on the track" I simply say that in my opening remarks I asked for the same privilege that was granted the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was permitted to wander in any direction he chose without one word being uttered on that side of the house, without one word from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) who consistently rises in his place and tries to impose regulation on members on this side while members of his own party wander free and easy wherever they choose. The member who sits in his seat and hollers "get back on the track" should have been here to see the example set by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, an example which, if the Chair permits, I will follow. I would appreciate it very much if members on that side would not sit in their seats and insist on hollering and trying to direct speakers on this side in the direction they would like to see them go rather than allowing them to follow the example set by their own minister.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, this debate was thrown wide open by the complete disregard of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the ruling of the house as to what form the debate should follow. You say "get back on the track". That is a very difficult thing for this government to do because they have not found a track to travel on.
With respect to the presentation of this resolution to the house, it is my opinion that prior knowledge was given to members on that side so as to permit them to make what they considered bold statements back in their own ridings. I refer now to the members from the Halifax constituency in particular. Prior to the resolution being presented to the house these members made big, bold statements as to what their stand was going to be on the flag and under what conditions they would vote for the three maple leaves flag. I say that in my opinion they had prior knowledge. I am also going to say something factual about one of the cabinet ministers. I must say there are not too many of them here, but among those present-
More than usual.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce indicates there are six. When you consider that the present cabinet is the largest and most expensive the country has ever had, six is not a great number. He should signal behind his back, not in front of himself.
There is the seventh.

If there are six present I am going to make a statement for you gentlemen, and each one of you if you wish can get up and deny having anything to do with this. Nevertheless this statement is being made by me as a factual one. The house will recall the answers that opposition members received prior to the very secretive introduction of the flag resolution. Nobody was allowed to know what the flag resolution was going to contain. Nobody was allowed to know what the design was. It was a deep, dark secret which, as I said before, in my opinion was revealed to the Halifax members at least so that they could make these bold statements.
I say to the ministers of the crown who are present now that from the mouth of one of the ministers I heard him take exception to the choice of the three maple leaves and in taking exception to the three maple leaves flag, which was presented by the government a couple of days later, he also indicated what his personal choice was. In my opinion this was tantamount to a leak because the opposition was denied any indication of what the design of the flag would be before the resolution came before the house.
Start bailing your boat.

I hear an interjection from a member representing Halifax. I hope that as a member of parliament he will declare his stand. At least the member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Kennedy) has a very good indication of where one of his constituents stands. I say that prior knowledge was made available to members of the Liberal party. I say that this knowledge was made available by a member of the government prior to the presentation of the resolution and in my opinion he revealed something that the Prime Minister was trying to hide.

A few minutes ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) took great delight in trying to imply something other than what was meant by my remarks. I point out to him that it is my opinion also that the Minister of Transport played a great part-it may have taken upwards of two weeks-in introducing the resolution in this form. I should like to point out that this flag question was not outlined in the legislative program in the speech from the throne. However, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) introduced this flag question before the national convention of the Royal Canadian Legion on a Sunday evening. This organization has endeavoured at all times to keep politics out

Canadian Flag
of its deliberations. Nevertheless the Prime Minister took before this convention a very definite and very delicate political question. There was a great deal of criticism with regard to this action. On another occasion I raised a question of privilege concerning a cartoon appearing in the Ottawa Citizen with regard to this particular convention, in which the Liberal members took a great deal of delight although it depicted all legionnaires as a group of alcoholics with the exception of the Prime Minister. A few days following that this same newspaper was referred to on another question of privilege. With the support of this kind of yellow journalism, the Liberal party has been putting across its proposed flag design. I cannot recall the date, and I stand to be corrected, but I believe this same Prime Minister said he would not turn his back on the red ensign. Today the red ensign has been deliberately torn down in favour of the three maple leaf flag. The red ensign does not even appear as the second choice.
The convention at Winnipeg indicated quite clearly to the Liberal party and the Prime Minister that there was a great deal of dissatisfaction amongst the veterans of this country with his choice of a flag. Who are the members of the Liberal party? I noticed that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) was somewhat irritated by certain remarks in this debate, and I put the question to him directly: Does he feel he is more qualified to decide on a Canadian flag than some of the veterans who have served under this flag or some of the families who have lost loved ones in the service of this country? Does he think he is qualified to stand in this House of Commons and pass judgment on what these people should recognize as the Canadian flag? Is he more qualified than a private, corporal, sergeant or officer in the Canadian services who fought under this flag? Does he consider he should have a choice in this matter while Canadian citizens, many of whom are vet-terans, are denied an opportunity to express their opinion on what the Canadian flag should be? Does the minister honestly feel he should deny this opportunity to citizens of this country while he stands in this house and follows the dictates of his Prime Minister? I almost said "his party", but that would have been a mistake because it has been indicated to me already by a highly placed cabinet minister of the government that he is not in favour of the three maple leaf flag. While expressing his opposition to the three

maple leaf flag, he indicated to me what his choice would be.
Now, here we have a highly placed minister of the crown who has clearly indicated his opposition to this maple leaf design. If the minister is present and wishes to deny it or if he sees these remarks in Hansard tomorrow and wishes to deny it, or if each minister wishes to get up I will take each and every minister off the hook in turn and then I will face the responsible minister with it. I will make the accusation in the house and tell him where and when he said it. I will tell the house what his alternative choice would be. I will remind the Prime Minister, then, that his cabinet is still divided on the choice of a flag. This information came to me from a highly placed cabinet minister. I say to the Minister of Forestry again, does he feel he is qualified to stand up in this house and vote on this issue when he denies the citizens across this country who are rightfully concerned the opportunity to express an opinion as to what the flag of this country should be?

PROVISION OF DIRECT SERVICE FROM NOVA SCOTIA TO BERMUDA
speechtext:
It is with a feeling of true humility that I attempt to follow the previous speaker but I will try to show in the course of my remarks the same fine spirit of moderation and co-operation as he displayed.
My question to the Minister of Transport this afternoon dealt with the provision of a direct air service between Nova Scotia and Bermuda, with connecting flights to the rest of the Caribbean and other parts of the commonwealth in that hemisphere.

subtopic: PROVISION OF DIRECT SERVICE FROM NOVA SCOTIA TO BERMUDA
speechtext: Don't forget the Virgins.

subtopic: PROVISION OF DIRECT SERVICE FROM NOVA SCOTIA TO BERMUDA
speechtext:
My question had reference to the fact that in Nova Scotia in particular, and indeed in the other Atlantic provinces, there has been a long and historic trade relationship and much intercourse with these areas. The volume of trade over the years has been impressive and as a consequence, my people have had occasion to go back and forth quite frequently. It is most unjust, therefore, that maritimers wishing to fly to Bermuda and on to the Bahamas and other points in the Caribbean should have to travel by way of Montreal and Toronto. Not only have we had this close relationship for many years but we have a geographic proximity to this area which is not enjoyed by the rest of Canada.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
We know Air Canada has been considering the introduction of a service from the Halifax international airport to Bermuda and I also know that when consideration is being given to this matter much is made of the volume of business which could be expected from such a service in the early years. I wish to suggest that when the officials of Air Canada are considering this matter they should bear in mind that the amount of traffic which they estimated for the Toronto-Nassau route turned out to be way below what was actually realized and that it has grown year by year. I think the service from Halifax would pay its way almost from the start, particularly if aircraft such as the Vanguard, which can also carry freight, were used. Such a service would enable lobsters from Nova Scotia, and possibly from other maritime provinces, to find a ready market in Bermuda or elsewhere in the West Indies.
We are told that one of the obstacles to the integration of such a service is that the British would demand reciprocity. In other words, they would have the right to put in a flight to some other part of Canada. I think the disadvantages of this are overestimated. Even if the British were to be given a flight to some other part of this country, the route from Halifax to Bermuda would soon become a popular and profitable route for Air Canada. If Air Canada is not interested in such a proposition, I suggest that Canadian Pacific Airlines or Eastern Provincial Airlines or B.O.A.C. might well be interested. It is not good enough that the people of the maritime provinces who wish to travel to Bermuda or to the Bahamas should have to go by way of Montreal or Toronto.
We will listen with great interest to the answer which the minister gives on this subject. The time has come when this service should be inaugurated. Indeed, it is long past. As a matter of fact we hope the minister will be able to announce that it will be brought into being in time for people from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island to use it during the coming winter, instead of being obliged to travel extra miles and spend extra dollars routing around Montreal.

I am glad the hon. gentleman was not allowed to receive the somewhat laconic answer I would have been obliged to have given him, under our rules, earlier today. It is hard for many people to understand why a service which would obviously be so beneficial should not be provided.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that the service would pay almost from the outset, particularly if, as he suggested, an aircraft such as the Vanguard were used which could carry a considerable quantity of freight. In that case there might be a great deal of two-way traffic.
There is, however, one problem, and it is a problem which is under active consideration by the air transport board at the present time. That is the problem of the bilateral agreement we have with the United Kingdom. Bermuda is a dependency of the United Kingdom, and we would have to renegotiate our arrangements with the United Kingdom; and they, not unlike us in this respect, are anxious to make as good a bargain for themselves as they can. There is not any doubt that they would ask for, and would be justified in asking for, some concession from us in regard to their services to Canada.
I do not set this up as an insuperable obstacle, but it is the kind of consideration that has to be taken into account in matters of this kind. I know that T.C.A.-in fact I know it very well, because I asked them to do it-are at the present time giving active consideration to the amount of traffic they can reasonably expect on this service, and they have not reached any final view about this; at least, they had not reached any final view

the last time I inquired, which was two or three weeks ago. But I would think, Mr. Speaker, there would not be any doubt that before very long this service would be a very profitable one.
I would hope, of course, it would not be just from Halifax but would be a continuous flight from St. John's-
